speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: MONTREAL
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the Prime Minister whether in view of the fact that the ultimatum issued by the C.B.C. to its producers in Montreal expires today, and in view of the most undesirable consequences of the implementation of this ultimatum on French language broadcasting, he would not intervene even at this late date in an effort to avert these unhappy consequences.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
subtopic: MONTREAL
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the question will be answered by the minister who reports to parliament in respect of the C.B.C.

speakeroldname: Hon. George C. Nowlan (Minister of National Revenue):
subtopic: MONTREAL
speechtext:
I am not aware of any such ultimatum as the hon. gentleman mentioned. There were discussions going on until four o'clock yesterday morning and, I know, during the night, and I understand there were also discussions going on last night. I have not been advised this morning of the situation. This is a matter entirely in the hands of the management of the corporation. In view of certain reports I heard yesterday I should like to make it clear that any steps which might be taken to bring this matter to a head were decided upon last week in consultation with the officers there, and there is no intention of delivering any ultimatum whatsoever; but sooner or later this matter must be brought to a head. I am told by the corporation that this was the plan of Mr. Ouimet, and this was the matter he was working on at the time of his collapse on Sunday.
The house will be glad to know that he is resting reasonably comfortably considering the very severe attack he had, and there is every reason to hope that if his present condition continues for a few more days he will be restored to health.

subtopic: MONTREAL
speechtext:
I wonder if I may ask a supplementary question. Since this unfortunate dispute has continued for
some time, could the minister say on behalf of the government rather than in the capacity as reporting for the C.B.C. whether the government or any ministers have considered making their good offices available for bringing the parties together so this dispute might be settled? There are many precedents for this being done in other instances affecting government corporations.

subtopic: MONTREAL
speechtext:
The government has not
given any consideration to this whatsoever. This is a matter for the management and staff of the corporation. The suggestion certainly has been made. There were 15 different proposals, I am told, 15 suggestions made by the management to the producers, every one of which was refused. The primary suggestion was to go to the Canada labour relations board and deal with that board and obtain recognition, and that also was refused. The management feel in the circumstances that there is no further suggestion they can make, but they are very happy to welcome any suggestion that might be advanced by the producers.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY

speechtext: The house resumed, from Wednesday, January 21, consideration of the motion of Mr. W. H. Jorgenson for an address to His Excellency the Governor General in reply to his speech at the opening of the session, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Pearson, and the amendment to the amendment of Mr. Argue.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
When the six o'clock adjournment interrupted proceedings last night, Mr. Speaker, I was expressing surprise at the gloom we have heard from the opposition in the last few days. It seemed to me that they are viewing with alarm on all sides, and I do not believe

The Address-Miss Aitken they are speaking for the people of Canada when they express this gloom. Certainly pessimism is not a characteristic of Canadians and, as the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill) said yesterday, Canadians are today greatly inspired by the prospects of a glorious future and are certainly ready to follow the inspired leadership of the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) and his cabinet.
There are three or four items in the speech from the throne on which I want to touch briefly. We are informed that we are to be asked to pass a bill of rights. Ever since the Prime Minister announced last year that he was going to introduce a bill of rights, lawyers have been having a heyday with it, arguing over all kinds of legal and jurisdictional difficulties between the federal and provincial governments. Like all other hon. members of this house I have been inundated with briefs, submissions and letters pro and con a bill of rights. I remember that last year the Prime Minister asked the people of Canada to give some thought to this proposal, and they certainly have done so.
I welcome the introduction of a bill of rights for two basic reasons. First of all, as I have said in this house before, it seems to me it is a good thing for all of us to take time occasionally to assess and evaluate the freedoms that we cherish. It is a good thing to stop and spell out democracy as we see it. The second reason that I welcome a bill of rights is that we of the western world can certainly do a much better job than we are doing of selling democracy. We take too much for granted in the rights and freedoms that we enjoy, and we expect other people in other parts of the world to take them for granted also.
The Prime Minister made a speech in Toronto recently when the University of Toronto bestowed an honorary degree upon him. He warned us all that democracy is losing the struggle for the minds of men in Asia and in other undeveloped areas. I think democracy is losing the struggle because we are not highlighting those things of the mind, heart and spirit that mean so much to us in democracy. Hence for those two reasons I welcome a bill of rights so that we may tell the world about the freedoms we enjoy.
Mr. Speaker, I address my next point to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) and the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan). In raising this matter I am probably speaking with a minority voice in this house. However, I believe there is existing an incongruous and discriminatory tax situation and that it should be corrected. I refer

to what is informally called the cosmetic tax, which is a 10 per cent excise tax. It is incongruous because presumably cosmetics are considered to be luxuries. They may have been luxuries at one time, but they are certainly not luxuries any more. Who would call toothpaste a luxury, or baby oils and powder, or shaving cream or shampoo and hand lotions?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: And lipstick.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Yes, I include lipstick in this list. I do not expect hon. members in this house to agree with me that lipstick is a necessity, not a luxury, but I believe that half the electors in this country would agree wholeheartedly.
Curiously enough the previous government removed this 10 per cent excise tax from several items but left it on cosmetics. The items that were removed from the incidence of the tax are ones which I consider to be luxuries such as fishing rods, cameras, golf clubs and soft drinks. However, the tax was retained on toothpastes, mouthwashes, medicated creams and many other items essential to good health and good grooming. I draw this matter to the attention of the Minister of Finance and the Minister of National Revenue in the hope that they will review this incongruous situation and remedy it.
In the speech from the throne there is promise of certain amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act. I do not know what those amendments are going to be, but I am sure they will be good and beneficial ones. There is one matter, however, that bothers me about the unemployment insurance benefits, and I am going to present this problem to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr). In the past, many times and oft, we in the Conservative party raised our voices against extravagances of the previous government. One glaring extravagance was the continual flow of publicity releases and pamphlets that poured from the various government departments. I am happy to note that this government has cut down a great deal on that flow. As a journalist I know what a waste it was, because these things would come into newspaper offices and simply be thrown into wastepaper baskets unread. However, at the risk of being paradoxical I am now asking the Minister of Labour to start a publicity project of his own or, as it may be more properly described, an educational program on the real purposes of unemployment insurance.
As I see it, unemployment insurance is insurance against the misfortune of being unemployed. But to be unemployed is not the real misfortune. To be unemployed and

unable to find work is the real misfortune. I feel that there is a wrong concept about this matter of unemployment insurance. People who take out automobile insurance are only too happy to assert that throughout their life they have never had to make a claim, and they certainly do not expect to get anything back from it. People who take out health insurance are only too happy that they are not obliged to make a claim for hospital care, and they do not expect to get anything back. But there seems to be a different concept about unemployment insurance. Far too many people appear to feel that since they have paid into this unemployment insurance fund, it is a sort of pension which must come to them sooner or later.
I should like to give three examples of what can and does happen with respect to unemployment insurance. Case No. 1 is that of an older woman who retired with a fairly substantial pension. She had paid into the unemployment insurance fund all her life and felt that it owed her something. When she retired she regarded herself as unemployed, applied for unemployment insurance benefits and obtained them. I do not believe that the unemployment insurance benefits were ever meant to be a sort of supplement to a retirement pension.
Case No. 2 is that of a young woman who had a highly specialized job but lost it. She applied for the same kind of job knowing full well, I am sure, that those jobs were not available. She was not able to get such a job, and she was quite happy to stay home and collect unemployment benefits.
Case No. 3 is that of a woman office worker who decided to stop working. Her husband was quite able to support her. Someone told her to be sure to get from her employer a letter to the effect that her services were no longer needed. He, I suppose trying to be a good fellow, gave her that letter and she collected her unemployment benefits.
I have given these three examples of the way in which I think this really great social security measure is being abused. I am sorry that all my examples happen to be women. I am quite sure there are an equal number of men. There may be hundreds or there may be thousands of such cases. They are all on the unemployment list and are included Jn the figures that we hear so much about these days. Our stand is this. We came into office on June 21, 1957. We saw the situation. We analysed it. We took immediate and positive action to deal with that situation, and our action has been effective within the limits of any action which can be undertaken by a government dealing with a situation which has worldwide ramifications and repercussions. The consensus of commentators and analysts not only in Canada but in other countries is that the action we took was wise and effective, and in this respect we came off better than the United States.
In proof of this contention I should like to read a number of sentences from Labour Research, a publication of the Canadian Labour Congress for June, July and August. First I should like to read this sentence:
The recession now seems to have hit bottom, and recovery seems to have started.
Then, after dealing with the employment situation and quoting figures comparing Canada with the United States, the article expresses the opinion, "Manifestly, Canada has come off better here." The article ends by saying, "Here again, Canada came off better."

and I intend to show that the actions of the government have been positive and constructive in nature.
We recognized the situation in June of 1957. Unemployment was rising, there was no question about that; the figures proved it. This situation was complicated by a large volume of immigration. We took immediate steps to curb the flow of immigration in order to give us an opportunity to level off the economy so as to provide jobs for those immigrants. The action of the former government was to allow this mass of immigrants to come here and walk the streets of Canada, the land of milk and honey, without jobs.

In this connection I should like to point out that the effects of the recession were much more severely felt in the United States, and I have already quoted the comments which have been made on that point by Labour Research, the publication of the Canadian Labour Congress.
Among the immediate measures which were taken were the increases in the old age security benefits and the rise in pensions for veterans and blind persons, which had the effect of adding to the income of a great number of Canadians. Mr. Speaker, at one o'clock I was discussing the municipal incentive plan, and I was informing the house of the cooperation we were receiving from the provinces and municipalities in implementing this plan in order to provide work for Canadians. But I wish to say at this time that the attitude of the opposition toward this plan has been a negative destructive approach. It has been an attitude of carping criticism; of treating lightly the fact that some 20,000 people will be employed on site and some
40,000	off site. That has been their position right along, Mr. Speaker.
The Leader of the Opposition the other day delivered himself at some length of an analogy relating to newly married couples, and made the statement that the honeymoon was over. But I will say that his party and his approach remind me of an old maid screaming about a man under the bed. That is all they are doing, Mr. Speaker, just screaming. There has not been one constructive, positive suggestion so far. While they have been screaming, Mr. Speaker, this government has been taking action.
What actually has been the reception accorded our program, Mr. Speaker? There have been varying reactions. I will say that for the most part reactions across Canada have been positive and constructive, and there has been a readiness, indeed in most instances an eagerness, to take part in the plan which indicates the need of this sort of program at the municipal level. At the same time I should also like to indicate that

The Address-Mr. Starr the provinces have been wholehearted in their co-operation. The plan has been in effect now, from the practical point of view, for only a little over six weeks. At the present time applications are coming in at a rate which indicates that the result over the next few months will be fruitful and positive.
What has been the reaction amongst the commentators and analysts? For the information of the house, Mr. Speaker, and with your permission I should like for a few moments to dwell upon that point. I take the liberty at this time of referring to the Toronto Daily Star of December 27. In an editorial under the heading "A Good Start" the Star commented as follows:
By paying 50 per cent of the labour costs of municipal winter work projects the federal government has so far helped to create temporary jobs for 9,400 Canadians. While this is a small number against the 361,000 Canadians who are unemployed at last report it is an encouraging start all things considered. With improvements and additions the plan could become an important remedy for winter unemployment.
The showing is not bad considering that the municipalities had little time to prepare for it.
I should also like to refer to an article in the Montreal Gazette of December 30 under the heading "Record Construction Forecast". I quote:
Volume of construction in Canada in 1959 will exceed the record total of 7,100 million in 1958 by from 3 per cent to 5 per cent, Howard J. Ball, Kitchener, Ontario, president of the Canadian Construction Association, forecasts.
Like each successive year in the post-war period Mr. Ball said 1958 was the biggest construction year in Canada on record.
With the continuance of this trend in 1959 construction will retain its position as Canada's largest industry with a direct labour force of some 620,000.
The information I have from New Brunswick, Mr. Speaker, is that a record winter works program is under way there. The minister of labour in New Brunswick, Mr. Skaling, has announced more than 100 projects valued at $5 million are under way or about to be undertaken. In Nova Scotia the minister of labour, Hon. Stephen Pyke, has announced that several winter work projects amounting to $3,167,318 which will provide 127,322 man-days of work have been approved. Mr. Pyke has added that this is a direct result of efforts put forth by the federal and provincial governments to increase employment during the winter months.
In the city of Ottawa a very substantial winter work program is being undertaken, and it is pretty much the same in all major cities across Canada. In Winnipeg particularly, Mr. Speaker, the situation has assumed a very favourable appearance. From reports I have received both from the unemployment insurance commission and from the Winnipeg newspapers, the situation in

Winnipeg has greatly improved in the last year. I quote at this time from an article in the Winnipeg Free Press, a journal which I might say can hardly be considered as biased in favour of the present administration. On January 8, 1959, the Winnipeg Free Press said as follows:
Winnipeg is going back to work. Employment here has improved to such an extent that the number of job seekers at the end of 1958 was nearly 3,000 less than at the end of 1957 and this in spite of the fact that the total labour force is higher.
The Winnipeg Tribune of Thursday, January 1, said in a New Year's day editorial:
Indeed in the Winnipeg area the picture is considerably brighter than at this time last year.
I should like to quote another article which appeared in Time magazine, a well-known United States publication, on January 5:
As 1958 was soon to prove the gloom sayers were wrong . . . the nation survived a difficult year without falling into the vee-sloped chasm that threatened briefly to trap the United States. A part of the reason was the rapid turn around in the United States. Much more was Canada's own doing. The natural resilience and sensible hard work of a developing nation.
It was reasonable to expect that Canada's recession would be even worse than the slump in the United States. As it developed Canada's down turn was much the milder. Aside from the winter months unemployment hit a smaller proportion of the working forces than the United States. Industrial production sagged less sharply and recovered early.
I quote further from the article in Time magazine, Mr. Speaker:
A second major difference between Canada and the United States was the way government handled recession. Unlike the Eisenhower administration which decided against large-scale priming of the economic pumps John Diefenbaker's Tory government put more spending money in wage-earners' pockets with tax cuts, it increased social welfare payments and provided $43 million for the grain growers.
The most impressive help of all went to housing. The Tories pumped $350 million into mortgage loans for housing much as the United States helped its home-builders. While the United States aid was largely a spot injection to help a particular depressed industry Canada's program was a vitamin pill for the entire economy. In the biggest boom in history 160,000 new homes were started, providing jobs directly to some 250,000 workers and touching off subsidiary booms in a dozen home supply industries. Another area where the government helped was in the outpouring of funds for defence. For Canada consumers all this and more money than ever before to save, spend or just jingle in their jeans.
I continue to quote from Time magazine:
Going into 1959 Canada still faces some knotty problems.

praise into the mouth of Her Majesty's representative. To me, it practically amounts to dragging the Queen's representative into politics. It seems to me that, while retaining the principle of the speech from the throne, we could ask the Queen's representative to come to parliament, welcome members in his words and pray God to guide them. Prime Minister could move a vote of thanks, seconded by the Leader of the Opposition, and right after the unanimous adoption of this motion, the government could place before the house the legislative program planned for the session.

Thus, the crown would keep its prerogative of making a speech from the throne, without being forced to praise the achievements of the government, be it Liberal or Conservative.

My P.M., My Government
My Ministers-My Word!

The Prime Minister said: "We have faced the problems as they came up". It is precisely about this that the Leader of the Opposition chided the leader of the government and the government itself. Instead of having prepared a program, instead of having foreseen what was coming, they waited until the worse came, and then they tried to put up with the situation as best they could. It is precisely what we had against him, and the Prime Minister admitted it himself when he stated: "We faced the problems as they came up." Now there is an old principle which says that "to govern is to foresee". As the present government cannot foresee, one must conclude that it does not know how to govern. Its policy is one of drifting, a policy of doing the indefensible. That is why ministers opposite have so much trouble trying to defend this policy. And we are being told that the duty of the opposition consists, as stated by the Minister of Labour, in suggesting to the government what has to be done.


Well, if we read over the speeches made by all those who were here in the opposition before the Conservative party came to power, including those of the Minister of Agriculture, we realize that they were merely destructive in their criticism, and that they never offered any suggestion that could be of any help to the government. That is what they have done, and we had nothing against that; today we have the right to adopt the same method, the same means.
As stated by the Leader of the Opposition after the convention where he was chosen leader of his party, the role of the opposition is to fight and to criticize the government. Our attitude has been the same as the Prime Minister's at the time he was leader of the opposition. We are going to fight and criticize the government; furthermore, we are going to remind it that it is not keeping its promises. We were promised that the country's evils would be remedied. During the election campaign, we did not hear the Liberal party being reproached for what it had done in the past. We were told that the Conservatives would cure the evils that now beset this country. That is why I say to the Prime Minister, and to those around him: now is the time for action. Put up or shut up.
I have here an article or rather an excerpt from an article by Mr. MacDonald in the Canadian Commentator. It says this:
During the first few months of 1959, the eyes of Canada will be turned on Ottawa, watching the discussions of a party strong in power but wavering in principle.
That is exactly what the Leader of the Opposition has said. Here is another article, this one from Le Droit, signed by the parliamentary correspondent Pierre Chaloult, to this effect:
Mr. Diefenbaker knows more than anybody in this country that the time for promises is past; that the next months will be difficult ones; there will still be unemployment; that, if there is any hope of improvement in the fall, it should be explained meanwhile why Canada's domestic and foreign trade has slowed down. There should also be some explanation as to why the Americans, the British, the French, the Canadians and others cannot agree on everything and more particularly everything that has to do with the problems of collective security, while each nation's financial responsibilities are increasing instead of diminishing.
These are statements of people who cannot be called rabid followers of this or that party.
I see in the Citizen the following article written by Mr. Swanson:

The speech from the throne refers to the visit of Her Majesty. All Canadians are happy to know that our gracious sovereign will visit us next summer, and Canadians, especially the average citizens, hope that, during her trip, Her Majesty will be given a chance to get a bit closer to the people, because this is not a totalitarian country where people's lives are in danger. The Canadian people are disciplined, they love their sovereign, and want to take a close look at her. This visit of our sovereign should not be just for the "brass hats", while people are kept 200 feet away behind ropes.
I remember that, when I was mayor of the city of Hull, the Queen Mother came to see us. At the time the Secretary of State Department had asked us, had in fact ordered the R.C.M.P. to let no one but officials and guests into the city hall. When I entered that hall and felt its chill atmosphere, well, against the wishes of the Secretary of State-I admit this remissness today -I gave instructions that the public be allowed to enter city hall. We installed ropes to prevent Her Majesty from being too pressed by the crowd. And when she went by-
Mr. Speaker, I hear laughter from the hon. member for Roberval (Mr. Tremblay) and every time I hear his inane laughter, I wonder how it is that a Canadian university could hire as a professor a man of this stamp. He should stand up so that all may see his silly grin.

In the speech from the throne there was a reference to Berlin and to the difficult international situation. To my mind the Prime Minister and the other ministers were right to mention it, because we are living under constant tension and difficulties, throughout the world, far from disappearing, seem to be growing instead. The main reason for this state of affairs, is, I think, that there has been steady adherence to the old principle of pagan Rome: "If you want peace, prepare for war."
Oh, I do not want to say that we should neglect our defences. There must be a modicum of defence. If only we sought to apply the golden rule to our international and domestic relations, which Christ taught us when he was among us, we could spread some of the kindness which should grace man. I believe that in time we would succeed in making this a better world, where it would no longer be necessary to spend billions and billions for the country's defence. Those billions would be earmarked for the welfare of our population, and for those peoples in the world who now are suffering from hunger and from cold.
Reference is made in the speech from the throne to economic assistance to underdeveloped nations. Mr. Speaker, the Liberal party has always been in favour of helping under-developed countries. Yet, I recall that during a certain election campaign, our Conservative friends in the province of Quebec were shouting at the Ottawa Liberals: "Ottawa gives to foreigners." Well, since these people have been here, the federal government has increased subsidies and gifts under the Colombo plan. We have congratulated them for it and we still congratulate them. And even at the Montreal conference, I mean the commonwealth economic conference, I believe the Minister of

The Address-Mr. Caron Finance pledged himself to increase up to $700 million, over three years, the assistance we could give to under-developed countries, both within the commonwealth and in the rest of the world. And yet, not one of these gentlemen was heard criticizing what they formerly reproached the Liberals with doing. Ministers, no less than ordinary members, have kept mum on this matter. We all know that the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mrs. Fairclough), is a charming, sweet, amiable and agreeable person, whom we all like to meet; but we also know her to be ultra-British, and to be bodily in Canada, while her mind is in England. Well, Mr. Speaker, I think when we hear "God Save the Queen", we can only look upon it as an anthem purely designed for royalty. It is not even a national anthem. It is greater than a national anthem, for it sings the glories of royalty, and it is also a religious hymn, containing an appeal to divine guidance and the Lord's protection for our sovereign, whereas "O Canada" is truly a national anthem, since it sings the greatness of our country, a country that has now come of age.
Canada has come of age. No longer is it a colony as in the days of Sir John A. Macdonald, or even those of Sir Wilfrid Laurier. Today we can walk alone, unassisted, without being held by the hand. Not yet. Why? It is, I believe, be-

cause the Prime Minister has chosen his Quebec ministers among the yesmen, rather than men who are able to take a stand.
