Mr. Speaker, may I be so bold as to compliment you, not in the exact words of the poet but with a meaning somewhat similar, namely that I admire the way you keep your head while those around you are losing theirs.
To begin with, I wish to commend this government on having installed the simultaneous translation system. I had some doubts as to how it would work, but I for one am very happy to admit that I have enjoyed the simultaneous translation of speeches made by our French-speaking colleagues which I would have missed otherwise, nor would I have time to read the English translation the next day. I think it is a step that will really bring us up to date on everything that is said, and it will be understood by every one at the moment it is said.
I wish, not because it is a habit, to congratulate the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Jorgenson), the mover of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. He spoke as the voice of the farmer, and I have no doubt that his constituents are proud of him. I also wish to congratulate the hon. member for Montmagny-L'Islet (Mr. Fortin) on his maiden speech. By the way, owing to the simultaneous translation, I was able to follow it as he was speaking. His speech on unity was very timely in these days of stress and difficulty that the free world is facing. We must be united in order to be strong in Canada, and strength like charity begins at home. The place to start the principle of unity is right in this country. I congratulate the hon. member and I forecast a bright future for him in this assembly, as he has displayed eloquence, ability and far-sightedness.
I should like to congratulate the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) on the success he achieved on his tour of countries of the commonwealth. Regardless of the partisan feelings of some Canadians, I think we are all 66968-9-14
The Address-Mr. Mandziuk. proud of the triumphant reception that was accorded him wherever he went. I believe there is general agreement in Canada that he accomplished a great deal of good; consequently, as a result of his visits and his candid talks with the leaders of the different countries, we shall benefit. Expanding trade and markets of the world should be forthcoming to this country of ours.
I know that from some quarters criticism was directed against the Prime Minister for being out of the country, while those criticizing knew full well that a capable cabinet was left here to run the affairs of the country in his absence. Therefore, I would like, Mr. Speaker, if I am permitted, to put on the record a quotation from a foreign newspaper, shall I say, but a newspaper from across the border, namely the Christian Science Monitor, from the pen of Peter Lyne, parliamentary correspondent. The headline and article reads:
London Warmed by Diefenbaker
Climax of Mr. Diefenbaker's visit to the United Kingdom came in London on the night of November 4 when an audience of more than 6,000, including British Prime Minister Harold Macmillan, packed the Albert Hall to hear one of the most fervent and inspiring speeches delivered in a long while on the theme of how the British commonwealth has a tremendous role to play in hurling back the communist attempt to destroy the free world.
Mr. Diefenbaker as a personality has aroused great interest here and great hope. Millions of Britons have seen on T.V. this handsome, dynamic figure with the blazing eyes of a revivalist. They have been warmed by fresh evidence of this man's 100 per cent enthusiasm for the commonwealth.
Mr. Diefenbaker scorned the "little faithers". He called on his audience to "banish doubts". He said, "Speaking here in London in this shrine of freedom, I believe that this commonwealth has today a greater appointment with destiny than in all her glorious history".
I quote from the same article:
When Mr. Macmillan came to speak for Britain he said that from his first meeting with Mr. Diefenbaker he realized that here was a great man.
This in spite of the fact that the opposition tries to belittle him at every opportunity in this house and outside. Mr. Macmillan said: "Great because he has the one vital thing that any great man must have-faith." This, Mr. Speaker, is the opinion expressed in the press of our neighbours across the border.
At the outset I wish also to commend the opposition for its activities throughout the country since the last session. I think Canadians did want to hear what the Tories had done to them. Canadians, of course, were mildly interested to hear that there was a new party still in the incubator and therefore unnamed which, when it hatches, will wipe the Liberals from the political field in

The Address-Mr. Mandziuk Canada. The prophets of this new party say that the Liberals have had it. Canadians were no less interested to hear the challenge accepted by the Leader of the Opposition who stated that the Liberals have not had it and that there was no room for a third party in Canada. I am inclined to agree with him if we judge the matter by the results of the general election last March when one of the splinter groups was wiped out altogether and the other was badly depleted. But the electors of Springfield apparently considered that they both had had it and we know the results. They elected as their representative a member who supports the government and I take this opportunity of congratulating the hon. member and the constituents of Springfield for their good judgment.
There are many projected pieces of legislation outlined in the speech from the throne. I only intend to touch on a few of them. I am happy that the speech from the throne does not neglect agriculture and that additional legislation is forecast. One does not need to be a farmer or an agricultural expert to realize that we have a farm problem. The Leader of the Opposition admits that we have a farm problem, and I should like to quote from an article in the Winnipeg Free Press of October 6, 1958 where under the headline "Pearson Has No Immediate Farm Answer" there is the following:
Liberal leader Hon. Lester B. Pearson Friday admitted that farmers, caught in a "price-cost squeeze", have a problem but offered no immediate solution. "I recognize that a problem exists. It is clear that agriculture hasn't had a fair share of the income of this country in the last 10 or 15 years."
Who was in power ten or fifteen years ago? I am glad that the Leader of the Opposition recognizes that we have a farm problem, late as this recognition comes. I continue quoting from the same article:
The former external affairs minister said a special Liberal party committee will formulate a farm policy this winter.
We are looking forward to hearing what this farm policy is. But I am proud of the fact that the government realized that we had a farm problem and realized it from the day it took office in June, 1957. I do not want to be repetitious. I do not want to set out all the emergency legislation that was passed and all that was done by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Harkness), the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill) and other cabinet ministers in their respective departments. But I do want to point out that this party recognized that
[Mr. Mandziuk.)
the problem existed and put price stabilization legislation on the statute books under which the government is permitted to establish forward prices on the basis of production costs and, where necessary, assist the farmers of Canada through deficiency payments in order to bridge the gap between costs and prices. While the procedure is applied to a limited degree, we have reason to believe that the board has now had time to do the necessary research on costs of production and will give further relief to the agricultural economy.
In my personal and humble opinion it is economic nonsense to expect an individual or organization to dispose of his or their product without any regard to the cost of production. If the primary producers of Canada are obliged to do that very thing and in effect subsidize the consumer, surely they have a right to expect some assistance in the process.
We realize also that continued penetration of the world market is contingent upon our remaining competitive. Losing sight of this breeds a dangerous situation for Canada, and it is high time that labour and industry matched the resourcefulness and efficiency of the farmer in cutting costs to the bone. I am not thinking of the farmers of Marquette alone; I am thinking of the farmers of Canada. Let us, their representatives, try to understand them. They have been fooled so often, they have been misled so often, that today they are impatient, suspicious and distrustful.
A farmer may not be a bookkeeper or an accountant, and even if he is he has not the time to do much bookkeeping, but the farmer realizes that in 1958 it took as much land, as much seed and as much labour to grow 1,000 bushels of wheat as it took in 1948, ten years ago. He also realizes that it cost him more in 1958 to grow 1,000 bushels of wheat than it cost him in 1948, ten years ago, because of the higher cost of labour, the higher price of machinery and the higher cost of repairs.
But he realizes also that his 1,000 bushels of wheat do not buy the same quantity of processed or manufactured goods in 1958 as they did in 1948, ten years ago. Whether these products are from the mines, forests or waters or even if they are products he produces and then repurchases after they are processed, he has to pay a higher price for them. Let us, the farmers' representatives, try to understand them. Let us realize and admit that the prices received by the farmer for wheat during the last ten years have fallen 20 per cent, that the prices of the commodities he has to buy have risen 50 per cent, as some say, or

possibly less. That is a moot point. But the point is that we have a farm problem. I am happy that we took emergency steps to alleviate the situation.
I am happy also to note that in the speech from the throne there are indications that other steps will be taken to improve the plight of the primary producers. They trusted us. They sent us here to represent them. I am happy to note that the farmers, and particularly the western farmers, are not going to go into politics. I wish to point out that at its convention last December the Manitoba farm union decided against joining this new party which is still in the making. They almost unanimously refused to tie themselves up with the socialists. I think that this is a commendable step. According to press reports many farmers in Manitoba are surrendering their memberships in the C.C.F. party.
The farmer does have his problems, but he does not leave the farm. As I said, the farmer is desperate and, like a drowning man, he will clutch at a razor in order to try to save himself.
I have said before that labour and industry should try to match the resourcefulness and efficiency of the farmer. Let them cut their costs to the bone, and I am sure we can get rid of these spectres which are causing us so much concern, namely unemployment and inflation, and which have been with us for so long. I see the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) smiling.
Western agriculture and business, of course, will be pleased to note that the government will take some action to alleviate the discriminatory effects of the recent horizontal freight rate increase. This matter has caused the farmer a lot of concern. While the cumulative effect of the recent increases granted to railway workers and the resultant general freight rate increases are still not known, I might just cite one example of the effect of these things. A piece of machinery, if delivered from an eastern factory in Ontario to Manitoba will take a freight rate of $2.69 now as compared with $2.30, and that is a full 17 per cent increase. I am very happy to note that the government is going to try to remedy the situation.
I am sure that Canadians will welcome the statement in the speech from the throne that Canada will strive toward a settlement of outstanding issues that threaten peace. Who does not want peace? We all want peace. I am sure Canadians will welcome the statement that the government is concerned over the soviet attempt to abrogate or change the interallied agreement relating to Berlin. I am sure Canadians will welcome 66968-9-14i
The Address-Mr. Mandziuk the government's determination to strengthen NATO as a deterrent against further aggression. These are serious problems which face us and they should receive serious consideration, regardless of our party politics.
This reminds me of a statement made by Generalissimo Chiang Kai-shek on Formosa. May I be permitted, Mr. Speaker, to quote what this gentleman said?
Our role is to be the lighthouse of freedom- That is our role on Formosa.
-a beacon of free people giving hope to those who struggle to regain their freedom in whatever country they may be. Our constant effort must be to remain free and ready so as to hold out hope to others who are in chains.
The western world has so few bastions of freedom left that we must cling to Berlin, to Formosa, to South Korea and these other places. The offensive against us is not only on the economic front but on all fronts, including the military front if necessary. Canadians must be concerned over the mounting costs of our defence department. They are concerned also about our inability to buy the most expensive defensive weapons. We must rely on our neighbour to the south to assist us in that respect.
Not more than 20 years ago we in Canada thought we were absolutely safe from any invader. We thought our front line of defence was the Maginot line and the front line of offence was the river Rhine. We thought we were absolutely safe behind our frozen north. We felt so safe we did not even bother to claim sovereignty over many of the islands to the north of Canada. Today, this situation has changed. We are scanning the skies for an invasion which we hope will never come but which may come. With the help of the United States, we have built the D.E.W. line. It was a costly affair, and it is going to be even more costly to set up more proper defences.
Now, against whom are we spending all this money? Why are we making all these sacrifices? Against whom are we preparing to defend ourselves? We might as well name the enemy we expect to attack us. We should know his habits. We should know his psychology. We should know his achievements in the past and his aims today. Let me, Mr. Speaker, take this house back a bit into history. Over 800 years ago in northeastern Europe a Slavic race was born called Muscovites. This race had the misfortune, from its birth to the present time, of never having the opportunity of learning the concepts of democracy, whether it was ruled by the autocratic, orthodox czar or whether it was ruled by the atheistic dictators of the Kremlin like Khrushchev. From the very

The Address-Mr. Mandziuk first they have applied an expansive and aggressive policy toward their neighbours, and once they conquered their neighbours they introduced a policy of persecution, oppression and political assimilation as well as economic exploitation. Out of the last 200 years the czars or atheistic dictators have devoted 128 years to aggressive wars and only 4J years to defensive wars.
If I may be permitted, Mr. Speaker, I should like to quote from words written 400 years ago by Dr. Giles Fletcher, the British ambassador to Russia, who wrote:
They (the subjects of the czars) are kept from travelling that they may learn nothing or see the fashions of the countries abroad.
Today these people behind the iron curtain are also kept from travelling abroad.
I quote again:
You shall seldom see a Russe a traveller except he bee with some embassadour or that he makes an escape out of his countrie which he can hardly doe by reason of the borders which are watched so narrowly and the punishment for any such attempt which is death if he has been taken and confiscation of all his goods.
Mr. Speaker, this can apply today to the people behind the iron curtain. I know constituents of mine, men whose wives have been left behind the iron curtain. They cannot get their wives or their children to this country. They cannot get permission from the soviet government to bring them in. The situation is that these communist dictators sitting on the czar's throne today ruling over most of Europe and over most of Asia are the ones whose claws or clutches we are afraid of lest they may bend across the north pole and invade us.
Mr. Speaker, it is with understandable emotion that I make reference to this day of January 22. Reference to it can be made only outside the iron curtain but cannot be made in the land of my fathers. Today, January 22, is independence day of the Ukraine. On January 22, 1919, after the fall of the czar's throne, a race of 40 million people after being persecuted, exploited and assimilated for several centuries broke their chains and declared themselves to be free. On January 22, 1919, at the ancient capital of Kiev, in the golden domed cathedral of St. Sophia, through its provisional government these people declared independence. This new republic of the Ukraine was recognized by Great Britain and France at the time. If the Ukraine were free she would be celebrating her forty-first independence day. .
Her fate was that of many other peoples who were incorporated into the imperialistic designs of the man or men who succeeded to the throne of the czars. The Ukraine republican army, owing to lack of armaments

and medical supplies-whereas the bolshevists inherited all the supplies and armaments they needed from the czar's army-were defeated after a bloody struggle of almost two years; and today you know where the Ukraine is. Only in a free world like Canada can her sons celebrate the event. Only there can survivors of the great days, comrades at arms who fought in that great liberation movement, get together and simply talk about the past.
But, Mr. Speaker, I am not losing sight of the fact that when the throne of the czars fell approximately fifteen other nations arose out of the ruins of the czar's empire. I mention the Baltic states of Estonia and Latvia -and I am speaking of the period right after the first world war-Lithuania and Poland. Poland with its glorious history regained its independence or declared its independence after or toward the end of the first world war. There were also white Ruthenia or Belorussia, Georgia, Armenia, Azerbaijan, Caucasia and others. As soon as the bolshevists had strengthened their hold on Moscow they started an aggressive war against all of the states that I have named.
I would say that only Poland and Lithuania and the Baltic states survived. The Ukraine and the others were all conquered back into the fold of a new dictator but of course not without a bloody struggle in each case. So, Mr. Speaker, Poland and Lithuania and the Baltic states survived. Czechoslovakia and Hungary rose on the ruins of the Austro-Hungarian empire. What have we today?
The dictators at Moscow have two classes of oppressed people. One class is those whom they want the world to call Russian peoples and those are fifteen different nations incorporated into the U.S.S.R. They want the world to know them as Russians. However, they are no more Russian people than we are in Canada. The other group are the satellites.
I am going to make a brief reference to those whom they want the world to call Russian peoples. The Baltic states of Latvia, Estonia, Lithuania, the Ukraine, white Ruthenia or Belorussia, and Caucasia, they want the world to know them as Russian peoples. They are people with a different language, different history, different customs and different background and are altogether different from the race that originated in northeastern Europe around their capital of Moscow. What a fallacy it is, Mr. Speaker, to call Ukrainians Russian people. It is about time the western world exploded that fallacy. I heard Mr. Mikoyan last Sunday on television. I know the Ukrainian language. I could not understand Mr. Mikoyan. Therefore my language and the language of my people and the language of the Russian people are different. We are different races. Our history is different.

The history of the Ukraine is 200 years older than is the history of Moscow. Our history is steeped in democratic tradition. Our princes intermarried with the royal houses of western Europe. The wife of Harold, who was defeated by William the Conqueror-I just do not remember the date-was a Ukrainian princess. At the same time her sister was the wife of the king of France.
Mr. Speaker, how about the Cossack republic of the Ukraine? When a hetman was elected, he could be deposed. It was a race steeped in democracy, a race that developed a different culture. We drew our religion from Constantinople, we drew our culture and our civilization from the west. What a fallacy to class Ukrainians as Russian people! I am mentioning this about the Ukraine because I am most familiar with Ukrainian history. But I have some knowledge of the history of Georgia, Azerbaijan, Lithuania, Estonia and Latvia and same applies to them. Some may say, "What are you complaining about? The Ukraine is a member of the United Nations." That is true, Mr. Speaker, but do you know why? After the revolution of 1917-1918 even the bolshevists could not erase the name of the Ukraine from the map of Europe, something which the czars had succeeded in doing. Soviets wanted to have a few extra votes in the United Nations assembly. Some may say, "Look at the constitution of the U.S.S.R. The Ukraine can secede, can get out of the union at will." Certainly that provision is in the constitution of the U.S.S.R. The Ukraine, as well as other countries-and there are fifteen of them incorporated into the U.S.S.R.- according to the constitution every one of them should be free to secede. Hungary is a satellite with a certain amount of autonomy. She asked for her freedom, and see what happened to her in 1956. All the so-called members of the free Union of Socialist Soviet Republics are free to have diplomatic intercourse with other nations. Have you ever heard of a Ukrainian ambassador to any country in this world? Have we got one in Ottawa? Have you heard of one from Georgia, from Lithuania or from white Ruthenia or Belorussia-that is another name? No. That constitution is just on paper, just to blind the western world.
There is that other group, the satellites. One would think the satellites were a bit more free behind the iron curtain, and to a certain extent they are. These people had held on to their independence from the end of the first world war, to the second world war, but are they free? Hungary asked for freedom and any Canadian's blood still boils at the thought of all these innocent, unarmed men and harmless women and children being
The Address-Mr. M. W. Martin crushed by soviet tanks. I am proud that Canada opened its doors and that Canadians opened their hearts to these Hungarian refugees.
What about Poland, that proud nation? Is Poland free? These people have a glorious history. These people were very powerful at one time. How is their church? How is it being persecuted? How free are they to secede and get out of the clutches of the soviet regime? How free is East Germany? Where are the free elections in any one of these satellites?
It is easy enough to ask the west to get out of Berlin. Is there anybody on earth who can ask Comrade Khrushchev to get out of East Germany? Is there anyone on earth powerful enough to ask him to get out of Poland, to get out of Hungary and to get out of the Ukraine? Is there? I throw out this challenge to the world. This is our potential enemy. This is why we are spending millions -to meet the insatiable greed of the dictator who has swallowed up most of Europe, most of Asia and extended his clutches towards the free democracies.
Mr. Speaker, I hope hon. members will forgive me if I was carried away. I warned them that the subject of the freedom of these peoples-a freedom which we can discuss in this free world-has certain emotional effects, more so, probably, since I am descended from a race which is 45 million strong and which is today behind the iron curtain. And the dictator wants to call them Russian people. The same applies to them all. There are 15 of them, as I have said. And the same applies to the satellites.
It is true enough that these people fought among themselves at some time or other in history, but I think they have learned their lesson and are prepared to bury the hatchet. I think they are prepared, when the time comes, to take up the call for freedom and work together. I do not hope for war. I do not want war. I do not want my son who is in the Canadian army right now to be sacrificed. But when the time comes-and God forbid it should come-I hope we are ready, I also hope that those people behind the iron curtain have not lost their will to live, because the dictator is trying to break their will and stamp out every thought of independence or freedom in their hearts or soul. I hope that they still have some of the fire for freedom burning in their hearts because they are our potential allies. If we forget that, we are lost.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, like the hon. member for Hull (Mr. Caron)' I am going to take advantage of the new arrangement making possible instantaneous

The Address-Mr. M. W. Martin translation. Normally I try to say a few words in the French language, but unfortunately I am still not as proficient in French as I am in English and I will therefore take advantage of this new invention and make my remarks in the English language.
I should like to add my congratulations to those which have already been extended to the mover (Mr. Jorgenson) and seconder (Mr. Fortin) of the address. I should like also to say a word about the remarks made by a couple of hon. members on the government side, in particular the hon. member for York-Scarborough (Mr. McGee) and the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Mandziuk), both of whom seemed to be very aware of certain newspaper reports which emanated from the province of Manitoba recently. I remember a newspaper report which emanated from Ottawa during the March campaign in which it was said that the Ontario C.C.F. party has resigned themselves to the fact that they were going to lose the Timmins seat to the Conservatives, and I suggest there is no more credence to be placed on the reports which they are reading now than there was at that time. In fact, I think it would be much more to their advantage if they referred to newspaper reports from the province of New Brunswick, because I see that a member of their party is reported as having said in the Ottawa Journal of January 8 as far back as December that he could no longer remain a supporter of the government and watch his constituents suffering because of the government's unfulfilled employment promises. So I think the government had better watch what is happening within its own ranks.
I was also interested in the announcement, after parliament has only been sitting for about a week, that two of our major problems have already been solved. I am referring again to the hon. member for York-Scarborough who indicated that something to the tune of 300,000 new jobs had been provided in the housing field, and of course, to the hon. member for Marquette who has solved the farm problem.
With regard to the provision of 300,000 jobs in housing, I should like to compliment the government. While I do not believe the hon. member's figure-he said it was a conservative estimate but I would be more inclined to think it was a Progressive Conservative estimate-I do think that this has been the government's most successful venture. This project to create more jobs in housing has, I believe, done more good than any other project on which the government has embarked.

As far as the hon. member for Marquette is concerned and his contention that the farm problem had been solved, on the face of it there is great difficulty in disputing that fact. Certainly the people in the farming riding of Springfield were not interested in sending a farmer down here. They preferred to send a dentist so we can only assume their problems are not too great.
The program of the government which has received the most attention this fall has been the program to relieve unemployment. When we examine it carefully I am afraid we must count it as an extremely severe disappointment. It has been said that as a result of this program 10,000 people would be provided with employment and various other figures have been cited. But certainly 10,000 in the face of present day unemployment is not much of a solution to the problem.
We have heard comments tossed back and forth across this chamber about the Liberal shelf of public works projects and that when the Conservatives got there the cupboard was bare and there was no tool kit and so they could not build one of their own. The limited attempt at introducing public works projects points up clearly one essential fact and it is that public works programs are not an adequate measure of relief for unemployment in this present day. Because of the changes that have transpired in the last 25 years hastily improvised programs of this nature are a most inadequate solution. The time has come when the government of Canada must devise new answers to this old problem. With machines taking the place of manpower in public works projects such as the building of roads, sewer lines and water lines these programs do not relieve unemployment to the extent that was possible a few years ago and I would suggest that the government cast about for new ideas in its efforts to seek relief for unemployment.
I should like to compliment the hon. member for York Centre (Mr. Stinson) and the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Morton) on the courageous way they brought into this house the comparative study on education standards in Canada and the Soviet union. I agree with the hon. gentlemen that the report reveals facts that should not be concealed. These are things that must be faced and I believe the Canadian people, if jarred to consciousness, will face up to the situation. I compliment the hon. gentlemen because this is a question which has held my interest for many years. Some hon. members may recall that when I made my maiden speech in this house as reported at page 191 of Hansard of October 27, 1957, my remarks were similar to those of the hon. members

to whom I have referred although my presentation of the situation was not as well documented as were theirs.
I have grown weary, as I believe many people in Canada have, of the everlasting bombardment across the floor of this house with the Liberals blaming the Conservatives and the Conservatives blaming the Liberals for every situation with which parliament is confronted. This type of behaviour is becoming stale and certainly it is accomplishing nothing in terms of solving present problems. I do not believe that the Canadian people, with the election three or four years away, are interested in hearing disputes concerning who is to blame for the present mess. The time of parliament would be better spent finding solutions to these questions. The government should not hide behind the fact that the opposition is prophesying gloom and doom whenever hon. members of the opposition point out weaknesses in the government's policies.
I wish to turn now to an urgent question that faces us at this time. I refer, of course, to the strike at the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation in Montreal extending over the past live or six weeks. I am convinced that this is more serious than many of us realize. While it produces English programs I am informed that the C.B.C. in Montreal is the largest producer of French language programs not just in Canada but the world. I think that many of us fail to appreciate that in producing these French programs the C.B.C. in Montreal is producing one-half of the Canadian culture in this medium. We have excellent studios in Toronto, Winnipeg, Vancouver and elsewhere but these produce only English programs, one-half of the Canadian culture in this field. After all, this is a bilingual country with a dual culture. Through the work of the C.B.C. Montreal studios Canadian television truly represents our culture in both its aspects.
This strike was not something that transpired overnight; there has been a long, steady process leading up to the present situation. Many of the producers concerned in this strike were in on the ground floor of the C.B.C. and built it up to what it is today, some of them working 16, 18 or 20 hours to make the network what it is. Slowly over the years there has also been built up on their part a sense of insecurity and frustration which is finding expression in this form. It has caused a section of management, in fact, to feel that in order to protect themselves they must organize along trade union lines.
To demonstrate that they are justified in doing so I wish to read an extract from the
The Address-Mr. M. W. Martin Quebec regulations, S.R.Q. 1941, chapter 162, article 2 of section 1, which states:
Twenty persons or more, Canadian citizens, engaged in the same profession, the same employment or in similar trades, or doing correlated work having for object the establishing of a determined product, may make and sign a memorandum setting forth their intention of forming an association or professional syndicate.
That is very clear. It is also clear that the real issue in this dispute is not wages or working conditions or the normal things we generally find in disputes of this nature. The point at issue is very clearly summed up by an article taken from L'Action Catho-lique as reported in the Ottawa Citizen of January 21, 1959, in these words:
The paper insisted that the crux of the problem was whether the right of association should be allowed. The paper also believed that the strike would open the public's eyes to the need for revamping labour legislation which, far from protecting the right of association, restrains it and in many cases even suppresses it.
That, Mr. Speaker, is the crux of the dispute: do they or do they not have the right of association. This strike has been honoured by many other unions involved in the membership of C.B.C. employees. I am informed that as recently as last evening one of these unions which refused to cross a picket line took a secret ballot among its members and 92 per cent still favoured not crossing the picket line and so endangering the keeping of the peace and possibly causing disturbances.
The latest move on the part of management in this case, that of intimidating the wives of these employees by sending telegrams and contacting them by telephone, is a move that is worthy of Mr. J. Y. Murdoch in his infamous strike at Murdochville but certainly is not worthy of this government or any of its crown corporations.
I would like to turn for a moment to some matters in my own riding. Again I would like to compliment the government on the fact that they left open the door this winter for the provinces to come in on a 50-50 basis with the federal government, which they did, on roads opening up new country. I am also very pleased that finally the Ontario provincial government has got around to taking advantage of this offer and at the present time roads are in process of being cut. I am thinking of the road between Foleyet and Chapleau, which will join the Porcupine goldmining area with Sault Ste. Marie and the United States across the new bridge. This is going to open up a vast new territory which will be a mecca for tourists.
At this time I should like to invite any hon. members, and particularly the hon. members on the government side, to visit my
208	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. M. W. Martin riding. Do not wait until prior to the next election before you come into my riding. You are welcome at any time. This part of the country is completely dotted with lakes, rivers and forests. It is a fishermen's paradise; it is filled with moose. Moose is one of the greatest exports we have in the north at the present time. This will also open up a loop by which American tourists can come up and visit the mining areas, and I am sure both United States and Canadian tourists will be interested in visiting the fabulous Porcupine gold-mining camp. Either this summer or the summer after will be an excellent time because the communities of South Porcupine and Porcupine will celebrate their fiftieth anniversary of the founding of the town during the summer and next year it will be followed by the town of Timmins itself.
Unfortunately, Mr. Speaker, there is one blot on the present optimistic outlook for the Porcupine area and it is one that this house should not only be interested in but, in fact, has a responsibility for. I, of course, am referring to the stand of the gold mines at the present time in the labour dispute which has been going on up in that area for two years. You may recall, Mr. Speaker, and probably hon. members will recall, the efforts of the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) and myself last year during the passage of the bill to amend the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act. We tried in every way possible to convince the government that it should keep a few strings attached to the increase in the gold subsidy. I think the evidence I can give the house today will prove that perhaps the government should have listened a little longer to us at that time. Oh, I recall, Mr. Speaker, that the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys (Mr. Comtois) quoted a letter as a final squelch last year to show that the government had in fact solved the problem up there. This letter is contained in Hansard of August 18, at page 3742. It includes the following resolution:
Proposed by H. Brunette
Seconded by W. Brewer
"That a letter of thanks and appreciation be sent to the Honourable Donald M. Fleming, Minister of Finance, and that this commission go on record on behalf of all gold mining communities of Canada in supporting the announcement of a 25 per cent increase in the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act, and that this commission is vitally interested in the longevity and continued extension of the said act on a longer term basis, so that gold mining communities may have a better opportunity for long-range planning."
Again, Honourable sir, we thank you and your colleagues, the federal government, for your kind interest in alleviating in some way the problem facing the citizens of gold mining communities.
One thing the minister forgot to mention that day, Mr. Speaker, was that the mover


of this motion was the brother of the defeated Conservative candidate and the seconder, Mr. W. Brewer, was the secretary of the Timmins Conservative association. Therefore, I do not know what sort of a letter they expected from those two gentlemen, but certainly they could not expect to get a very critical one.
The last time the gold miners in the Timmins area received an increase was away back in 1954, just at the completion of a strike of about eight months. Since that time the federal government has paid over $10 million in subsidies to the nine gold mines covered by the bargaining unit in Timmins; in fact, almost $5,750,000 to the two mines of Hollinger and McIntyre alone. As I said, that is since the last increase was given to the miners. As hon. members will recall, during the last session the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act was extended for another two years and a 25 per cent increase was also given, retroactive to the first of 1958. In all fairness to the members of the government I am sure that most of them thought, as most of the municipal officials and in fact the people of the Porcupine camp thought, that in making this move to assist the gold mining industry some of it would automatically brush off on the miners. Unfortunately, that has not happened. Despite this increase, despite this extension, not one cent has been offered to the miners in those nine mines covered by union agreements. At the Hollinger mine, for example, negotiations have been going on since September, 1957. Last year, following through the normal procedure of bargaining in this province, the miners took their case to a conciliation board and that board sat in Timmins in the month of June. As a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, they were sitting on the very day that the proposed increase was announced in this house.
This board did not make any snap decision. It weighed every factor very carefully; in fact, it sat on its report for a matter of three months. The report was not delivered until September of last year. I would like to list a few of the things recommended by the majority report of the conciliation board which was signed by the chairman and the union nominee:
X. Two-year agreement;
2.	Forty-two hour work week in the first year of the agreement and a 40-hour week incorporated in the second year of the agreement.
They are still working a 44-hour week in that area. I continue with the recommendations:
3.	Five cents per hour increase in pay and that this payment should be made retroactive.

This was to be at a time negotiated between the two parties. I continue:
And adjustments to be made upon the reduction of the work week, to guarantee no loss in pay.
4.	Four cents an hour shift differential for afternoon shift and six cents for night shift.
5.	A recommendation of six statutory holidays. With the recommendation that the holiday pay be the equivalent of 20 hours for eight hours work on such days.
6.	That there shall be an extra week vacation for a total of three for all employees with a total of 15 years or more seniority.
7.	The board recommended that a pension plan should be negotiated and to become effective on the second year of the two-year agreement.
Of course, they have no pension plan. I continue:
8.	The board recommends that the contribution to a medical plan would be on the 50-50 basis.
9.	The board recommends a check-off of union dues.
As you can very well imagine, they have no union security there. This was the recommendation of the conciliation board and it amounts to a package deal of well over 20 cents an hour. In that report the chairman had this to say:
In the opinion of many, the only real value from a report from a board of conciliation is to consider a likely, or at least possible, realm of settlement and to point out a position to which each party might come. With this in mind the only matters which have been considered in preparing this report are the ability of the company to pay and the adjustments which might be accepted by each party in an effort to decrease the discrepancies in monetary matters and working conditions which exist between these employees and those in industry in general in Ontario.
With reference to emergency gold mining assistance, when the act was originally passed it was supposed to be for the miners of the mining municipalities. That was the announced intention of the legislation. When the act was passed it was not supposed to be just for the gold mines. It has been stated on different occasions that its purpose is to assist gold mining municipalities. This is what the chairman of the board had to say:
This improvement was stated to be to promote the well-being of our northern gold mining communities. One can hardly comprehend the view of the commitment which does not also assist the employees living in the community, but only to the corporate entity which is geographically located.
The mines have just been granted a 25 per cent increase by the federal government and yet they refuse even to recognize the report of the board. They have refused even to discuss it or negotiate on the basis of it. So the union, in an effort to try to get things settled without having to go on strike again, voluntarily moved away from the report. The representatives of the union said, "All right, if you will not talk about that, what will you talk about?" A meeting was then held with
The Address-Mr. Webster the chief conciliation officer for Ontario but so far nothing has developed from the point of view of a settlement.
But here is something that has developed over these months which I think is of vital importance, particularly in view of the letter I mentioned a while ago which was put on Hansard last year by the minister. I have here a resolution passed by the Timmins town council on January 5, 1959. It was moved by McDonald and Burnette and, incidentally, Mr. Burnette is the defeated Conservative candidate. The resolution reads as follows:
That Timmins council go on record as supporting collective bargaining and suggest that management recognize collective bargaining and sit with the representatives of their employees and settle these disputes at the earliest possible date so that the uneasiness that prevails in this area at this moment be done away with.
Along the same lines, the union also had a meeting with the local member of the provincial legislature, who is minister of lands and forests in the Ontario government. From a report of the meeting in the Timmins Press of January 17, 1959, I read the following:
Lands and forests minister J. W. Spooner told a 16-man delegation of the united steelworkers of America last night he would meet with labour minister Daley and Louis Fine, chief conciliation officer, Monday, to urge them to request top management of McIntyre Porcupine Mines to negotiate with the union. Mr. Spooner referred to existing relations between the union and McIntyre. He said conditions "are not good for the workers involved or for the community". "There should be a willingness", he said, "on the part of parties involved to meet and negotiate. There should be no war of nerves."
Referring to collective bargaining, Mr. Spooner stated it is the law of the land-that should not be a question but should be understood by everyone.
That is the situation, Mr. Speaker. As I mentioned earlier, the miners have not received one cent of this increase that is supposed to benefit the gold mining communities. These nine mines have received over $10 million in such assistance. I say that it is the responsibility of members of the cabinet and all members of the house to use any influence they have in any way they can to see that the money which has been voted for this purpose winds up being used for the purpose for which it was intended in the first place.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, like others who have spoken before and, I am sure, like others who will follow me, I want to welcome as warmly as I can the new members who took their seats for the first time last Thursday. At least one of the new members has made a great contribution already in making the members of the house as a group easier to look at. I am
210	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Webster sure that in the months and years ahead all the new members will play a full role in the business of governing our country.
To one of them, the hon. member for Montmagny-L'Islet (Mr. Fortin), has already gone the honour of seconding the address in reply to the speech from the throne. As an English speaking member from the province of Quebec, I can only agree as strongly as possible with the sentiments regarding national unity so well expressed by him. In past years much lip service has been paid to national unity, and I think most of us will agree that since the war great improvements have taken place. I am proud to be a supporter of a government which is carrying this tradition forward in practical terms that will have everlasting benefits to the Canadian nation.
I must also congratulate the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Jorgenson) for his able and articulate speech in moving the address in reply to the speech from the throne.
January, as we all know, is the month both for looking forward and looking backward. Before discussing current affairs I think it only fair to congratulate the government and the house for the legislation processed during the last session. This legislation has been criticized in the past and is being criticized again during this debate. But I would remind my friends to my right and to your left, Mr. Speaker, that the people have already passed judgment on the work of the government and parliament. There have been four by-elections, and candidates who based their appeal on the policies of the Progressive Conservative party and the record of the government in its short period of office won three of the four elections. That is answer enough for the criticism but it is no reason for complacency on the part of the government or any member of the House of Commons.
The speech from the throne is evidence enough, I believe, that the government is not complacent. To my mind it is a workmanlike document. There is a lot of work ahead of us. But what impressed me most about the speech from the throne was the tone of confidence. The country and the government face many problems, many difficult decisions. But surely if the government was not confident how could it expect the people of the country to think, to work and act confidently?
Before I deal with other items, I know the people of St. Antoine-Westmount, whom I have the honour of representing in the house, would want me to express their pleasure in anticipating the visit of Queen Elizabeth and Prince Philip to this country for six weeks. We were pleased to note that Her Majesty is


going to be seen in areas in which no monarch has been seen before. The visit to the Yukon and Northwest Territories should be a great inspiration to the people on the Canadian frontier.
But, of course, we in Montreal were greatly gratified, despite some malicious rumours, to find that Her Majesty and Prince Philip will spend two days in our city. They will arrive and leave aboard the royal yacht Britannia, which serves to underline the great purpose of this visit and that is to open the St. Lawrence seaway. I was interested, as I am sure many Canadians were, in the suggestion of the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) on Tuesday that, if necessary, there should be two official ceremonies opening the seaway. I quite agree. I recognize the necessity of co-operating with the United States in some kind of international ceremony, no doubt along the international border. However, the seaway does begin at Montreal; much of the work was done along the south shore, and the seaway was developed by Canadian initiative. I think that this initiative, and our national pride, make it imperative that Her Majesty preside at some all-Canadian ceremony in the Montreal area.
I am glad to see that such wide use is being made of the Britannia in this tour. The progress of this beautiful yacht through to Chicago and the head of the lakes will dramatize to the world that Canada has a new coastline. It will also give to many of the lakeside communities a unique opportunity to be host to the Queen and her consort prince.
The seaway has always been important to Montreal, even when that particular stretch of water was only passable by canoe bringing furs to trade. Ever since Canada decided to go ahead with the construction of a 27-foot deep waterway there has been a great debate raging in Montreal. Fears have been expressed that much of the traffic which has been the backbone of Montreal's development and prosperity would pass the city by. But these, in my opinion, are short-sighted fears. The seaway will be a great spur to the development of the entire Canadian economy, and in a stronger and growing economy Montreal will have no place to go but up.
We, in Montreal, are pleased to see that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees) does not share the views of the pessimists. Montreal harbour is getting new piers, new grain elevators, new storage sheds and the deeper berths and turning basins required to share fully in the benefits of the seaway. As a result of the Queen's visit and the opening

of the seaway this is going to be a great year for Montreal and for Canada.
Mr. Speaker, we have already heard a great deal in this debate about the state of the Canadian economy. We have heard the government damned for not doing more about unemployment and damned, in almost the same breath, for not curbing inflationary tendencies. The opposition seems to want its cake and eat it too. When this government took office unemployment was already mounting and foreign trade was dropping off. Our trade deficit was higher than it had ever been before.
This government took the necessary steps, and today we see the results. The recession is ending with far less impact on the Canadian economy than it has had on other economies, peoples and their standards of living. Recovery has reached the point where many responsible authorities are talking about the threat of inflation. This talk is positive proof of the end of the recession. Winter unemployment, while still serious and worrisome, is showing a much slower rate of increase than it did last year. Our overseas trade is picking up.
In this connection I think we should note the benefits already flowing from the Montreal conference on trade and economic affairs. Trade barriers between Canada and the United Kingdom have been reduced and similar improvement can be expected in so far as other members of the commonwealth are concerned. This government gave notice then, and has repeated it in the speech from the throne, that it intends, on Canada's behalf, to continue shouldering the responsibility for increased economic assistance to the underdeveloped nations. The long term benefits of such a program are impossible to assess. We are meeting the communist threat of expansion on its own terms, and we are building the ability of other countries to become, in the years ahead, important customers of Canadian products.
If we should continue to trade only with countries enjoying roughly the same standards of living, then there could be no hope for less fortunate countries to improve themselves to the point where they may become important markets for our surplus products. We cannot remind ourselves too often, when we think of international trade, that we cannot get rich taking in each other's washing.
There is one other paragraph in the speech from the throne to which I should like to refer. It states, and I quote:
Discussions are taking place with the government of the United States to enable Canadian industry to share in the production of equipment being procured by the United States for joint defence purposes.
The Address-Mr. Webster
I noted with interest that the delegation from this house and the other place which was in Washington recently discussed this subject with members of the United States congress. There were some suggestions at that time, again I think by the hon. member for Laurier, for a revival of the Hyde Park wartime agreement. Under this agreement, negotiated as you will remember between the then prime minister, the Right Hon. Mackenzie King, and the then president, Franklin D. Roosevelt, the United States placed defence orders worth close to $1,500 million during the second world war. Some of us seem to have forgotten that the principles set out in the Hyde Park agreement were carried into the post-war period of reconstruction and conversion of industry to peacetime tasks. This was accomplished through an exchange of notes between Canada and the United States in 1945.
I want to underline that this did not supersede the Hyde Park agreement, but only carried the same principles forward. Then, five years later, in 1950, Canada and the United States agreed on a statement which has become known as the principles for economic co-operation. One of these principles is, in effect, that the United States and Canada should co-ordinate their requirements, their production and their procurement, to get the best production for common defence. These principles are still in effect, Mr. Speaker. There seems to me to be no need for any new statement of principles, the negotiation of which would only take much valuable time. I commend to the government a policy of underlining to the United States, in the most forceful terms possible, this 1950 statement of principles for economic co-operation.
There have been suggestions already that the actions of this government in demanding consideration for Canadian industry are having an effect in Washington. A story last week in the Financial Post set out that the Pentagon in Washington has asked its suppliers to let Canadian firms tender on the same basis as United States companies.
In Montreal we are hopeful, of course, that the United States will make a decision to buy the CL-44 aircraft developed by Canadair. The feeling is that this four-engined long range aircraft, a leader in its type, would be ideal for use as a picket radar plane carrying the radar warning system far out over the Atlantic flank of the North American defences.
There is one other item in the defence field which I feel should be underlined. I was happy to hear the Prime Minister (Mr. HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Webster Diefenbaker) refer on Monday night to lobbies. Too often I think Canadians, and particularly members of parliament, have been too sanctimonious. We like to think that there are not any lobbies in this country, that we are free of the odious reputation that has been attached to lobbies and their pressures on government in Washington. We all know this simply is not so. I think it is time this was made quite clear. Every one of us knows he is subjected to hard and repeated lobbying on every conceivable subject that comes before us and some that do not. We hear the excuse from the United States that powerful lobbies there would not stand for it if the Pentagon decided to order a Canadian fighter aircraft; that they influence decisions against Canadian lead and zinc producers and against Canada's gas and oil industry.
By admitting that we, too, have lobbies and pressures upon us here in Ottawa, I believe our bargaining hand with the United States will be strengthened. It is time that people both inside this country and outside it knew that there are in Canada pressure groups which must be reckoned with.
There are other topics in the throne speech with which I might deal, Mr. Speaker, but I should like to conclude with just one more thought. As members of parliament and as legislators we should find it interesting and valuable to check this speech from the throne against those of thirty years ago. Then this parliament seemed largely concerned with developing the physical assets of the country. Today we have before us a large body of legislation relating to improvements in the social welfare of our people. We are concerned too, of course, with the economic necessity of developing our natural resources to provide the strong economic base for these social welfare programs.
Canada is fortunate in its relative youth. As a result we have not had the same opportunities to waste our natural resources. Today we must be careful to see that these resources are developed, not primarily for the benefit of the few but for all the people and that they make a contribution to this country on which a better standard of living for everyone can be based.
With good planning, intelligent execution and the resources we have, Canada can remain and develop as one of the world's most prosperous nations. My hope for this session is that the work we accomplish here-the criticism heard and the defence made; the legislation discussed and passed-will contribute substantially and significantly to the achievement of this goal.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, rising today in this house, I join with the members who spoke before me in congratulating the mover and the seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne (Mr. Jorgenson and Mr. Fortin). Both, by the lofty tone of their speeches, and the ideas embodied in them, have given evidence of their ability.
The debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne gives members of this house an opportunity to make known to the government the needs of their constituency and the living conditions of the people they represent. It is for Canadians an invaluable opportunity which allows them to give an accounting of their needs and thus to contribute to the stability and security of Canada.
We live in a troubled world where peace is constantly threatened, and the most vital need of a nation is after all, to feel that within itself and in neighbouring countries there reign the peace and the security to which they are entitled. The previous government, like this government, has indeed made it its concern to give this nation peace and security and, jointly with other nations, to ensure world peace. I hope this government will continue to pursue this policy and that its efforts will soon be rewarded.
As I said a while ago, people need and crave peace. But international peace is not enough; one must feel within himself security and inner peace. The people of Canada want full employment. They want to earn a decent living for themselves and their families.
At this time, the country faces two very serious problems, unemployment and inflation. When the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) was making his speech, some ministers of this government asked him which of the two problems he considered the more serious. I must draw the attention of hon. gentlemen to the fact that it is not up to the Leader of the Opposition to dictate the government's policy because the government has been elected to administer the country's business, and to choose the necessary ways and means to remedy the prevailing uneasiness. We have known times when, under Liberal rule, there was some uneasiness affecting this country, and the government of the day took action to correct the situation.
We should keep in mind those four years, years of reconversion, when jobs had to be

provided for returning men. The Liberal government at that time administered the country's economy so that each could return to civilian life and easily find a job.
To ease unemployment, the government has suggested winter projects for which it undertakes to pay the municipalities half the wages required for such projects as sidewalks, streets, waterworks, sewers and municipal parks. Now are these projects practicable for all municipalities in Canada and, moreover, do those municipalities have the necessary funds to carry out this work?
Representing a riding of the city of Montreal, I do not hesitate to say that none of the projects listed by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr), in the brief he addressed to us on November 20 last, can be carried out.
The city of Montreal is now facing a problem of snow removal which absorbs all its energy and affects its budget. It is impossible to build sidewalks when there is a foot of snow on the ground. It is also impossible to lay sewers when the streets are bordered by seven foot snow banks and more snow is falling every day. It is impossible to clear park areas that have been filled with snow removed from the streets. Also, most of Quebec municipalities lack the means to undertake such work in winter because labour would be more expensive than in summer and the share put at their disposal by the federal government would be absorbed by the extra cost of labour.
The government is perfectly aware of the financial position of municipalities, and of their ability to pay, for it summoned them to a conference, here in Ottawa, last fall, to assess their needs; and nearly all of them told the government how hard-pressed they were for funds. This winter works program is but a second-rate stopgap for those who suffer, and will in no way relieve the present situation.
It is inconceivable that, in a country as rich as ours, there should still be people who have to beg for their daily bread and live in miserable conditions. In view of this alarming situation, His Eminence Cardinal Leger, Archbishop of Montreal, had really every reason to suggest the setting up of public works programs in order to alleviate the misery of those who are suffering, and to appeal to the charity of all citizens of Montreal to raise the funds required for the implementation of such projects.
This winter works program came too late for municipalities which wanted to take advantage of it to get ready for it. It was announced at the end of October by the
The Address-Mr. Meunier Prime Minister, and the municipalities got the government offer in writing only about two weeks later.
In the house, last July, when the estimates of the Minister of Labour were being voted, we pressed him with questions about his plans for the relief of unemployment during the coming winter. The hon. minister announced nothing. If he had then and there announced his program, the municipalities could have got ready and the jobs provided would have relieved the hardship now being suffered by my fellow citizens in the province of Quebec, especially in Montreal, where there are 80,000 unemployed.
The government also faces another paradoxical situation: inflation. While, on the one hand, unemployment is rife, prices are soaring and no one can tell where this dizzy rise will stop.
The government lacks a planned economy and a flexible policy to face the situation. In his annual report, the president of the Royal Bank of Canada refers to that inflation crisis in the following terms:
Last year, as in previous recession periods, when the economy was on the decline, I recommended tax and price cuts; now, instead of tax cuts which might have spurred business and lowered prices there has been an increase in government expenditures expenses.
In fact, it is to be wondered whether these government expenditures have not contributed to inflation.
Last year, during the 1957 session, the government had hundreds of millions of dollars voted for home building, believing that such expenditures would relieve unemployment and improve the standard of living of the people of Canada.
There is no doubt that this industry has achieved part of its objective, but it is none the less true that the price of land, and of materials, has increased to such an extent that the selling price of a house has become a problem for the builder. Besides, Mr. Speaker, new housing has become so expensive for the builder that he has to rent it, and cannot find a buyer because he is asking too big a price for it. Yet he has to rent it at that price if he wants to break even.
In his report on the matter the deputy minister of Public works says that the building industry has increased its production in a spectacular way. On the other hand, Mr. W. N. Shortill, chairman of the Toronto Real Estate Board, also expressed his opinion on the matter, which may be found in the Gazette of January 15 last, when he stated that it is getting harder to sell a house. Mr. Shortill claims that there will be competition in the
214	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Meunier sale of houses, because the supply is greater than the demand. He claims that there is bound to be a price war in the sale of houses, if building construction is carried on on the same basis in 1959 as it was in 1958.
All those government expenditures have caused inflation and, in my opinion, the government would have been better off in building a limited number of houses each year instead of creating surplus which we now have. In Montreal, many builders have stopped operating because they can't sell the houses they built last summer. I hope the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) will follow up the statement he made recently, to the effect that he would fight inflation by cutting down on government expenditures.
This government does not seem to be alarmed at budget deficits. Thus Monday night, I heard the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefen-baker) mention that from 1935 to 1957, while the Liberal party was in power, there had been
14	deficits. However, there are justifiable deficits, and others that give cause for alarm. Those mentioned by the Prime Minister under the Liberal administration included years of depression and years of war. At the moment, the country is in the throes of inflation, yet the government records the greatest deficit in Canada's history.
Mr. Speaker, I will only say that the speech from the throne mentions nothing that could give hope to Canadians that the present situation will be corrected.
The Prime Minister recently made a trip, but he has not said yet whether, as a result of the meetings he had during this trip, other markets will be opened to Canadian products. Canada needs an expansion policy, the opening of new markets to sell its products.
Like other members who spoke before me, Mr. Speaker, I heard and read with interest the speech from the member for Mont-magny-L'Islet (Mr. Fortin). If Quebec is a province like any other, it must play its part in the confederation and co-operate to the greatness of the country.
Since the seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne is in a co-operative mood I am sure that he will make use of his resources to settle the thorny issues that have come up between the province of Quebec and the federal government for some
15	years.
These are matters of vital importance and they cannot be neglected indefinitely. The matter of grants to universities is an urgent


one. If we want those institutions to achieve the goal for which they were founded, the matter must be settled soon. We all know that education is a provincial matter, but it seems that a grant or aid given unconditionally for the cultural development of a nation does not infringe upon its rights and prerogatives.
The province of Quebec is also interested in the problems of health insurance. If the former federal government initiated this social measure, and if the present government has implemented it, it is because it was a good measure and because the people of Canada wanted it.
Several provinces have joined in, but the province of Quebec has not yet said what it proposes to do in this regard. The people of Quebec, like those of all other provinces, pay heavily for hospital services and provincial participation in this plan would relieve Quebec taxpayers.
The speech from the throne also tells us that further funds will be required for the completion of the trans-Canada highway. This is another question which has been eliciting a negative answer from the province of Quebec for almost 10 years. Is that highway, started by the Liberal government, and which this government is still building, of any use to this country? It is unmistakeably useful in wartime as well as in peace time, and if those amounts of money were used in the province of Quebec, they would alleviate hardship and could provide work for many jobless.
For all those nationwide projects, the Quebec taxpayer has been paying taxes and it is only fair that they should bring dividends to him in improvements which will ensure his security and welfare.
I grant that the opponents of such projects use arguments of questionable validity, but if everybody sticks to his guns and never tries to reach an agreement or an honourable compromise, the population in a province will be indefinitely deprived of invaluable advantages.
If the intention is to play politics with those issues forever, to make a political football out of them and to appeal consistently to emotion, the Quebec taxpayer will in the long run be the loser and feel cheated of his rights.
Again I submit, Mr. Speaker, that none of those matters will be settled by a negative approach, and that among people of good will you can reach an agreement without disregarding fundamental principles.

Another point I should like to mention in my remarks, Mr. Speaker, has to do with the Canadian contribution to the Colombo plan.
Of course we must help underdeveloped countries to build up their economy and, later on, when their expansion is in full swing they will be able to become customers on the international market where we can dispose of our products.
This year, Canada undertook to provide $50 million under this plan. Can we really afford this expenditure, or is Canada making commitments out of all proportions to its finances?
I know that under the Liberal government, when contributions were of the order of 8, 10 and 12 million dollars, Quebec Conservatives criticized these gifts, and labelled them extravagant. I wonder what their attitude is today. Perhaps, in the light of the facts shown to them their opinion has changed, but it would be interesting to know their stand on this matter.
There is also, Mr. Speaker, another matter that I would like to take up with the house, particularly with the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan), and I refer to the C.B.C. producers' strike in Montreal. We know that the C.B.C. enjoys independent status but is answerable to the Minister of National Revenue. The strike has gone on since December 29, and it appears that neither party is ready to reach agreement with the other. We know that the producers want to have their right of association recognized and that the C.B.C. refuses, on the grounds that they are part of management. We cannot know who is right, because of the little information we have on the matter, but it seems that the minister could at least step in and try to settle the dispute which is crippling the network and depriving part of Quebec people of favourite TV programs.
Several previous speakers have said that the government has no coordinated and definite policy. This is causing concern to the public and besides, it seems that certain cabinet members are making irresponsible statements and spreading confusion on many matters.
Canada has made much headway these last 25 years in the field of national unity, and no one has worked harder and more sincerely to this end than the former Liberal prime minister, the Right Hon. Louis S. St. Laurent.
Now, it happened that, quite recently, two government ministers have made the statement that our national anthem is God Save
The Address-Mr. Bourdages the Queen. They know perfectly well, however, that Canada has no law nor statute to confirm this. I very much admire our gracious Queen and I like to sing her anthem when it is proper to do so, but it seems to me that when a fact is not clearly established, one must be careful not to wound feelings or create confusion in order to belittle another anthem highly considered throughout Canada and even abroad.
I say abroad because I remember the statement made by the Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent, here in this house, on March 18, 1954, which appears in Hansard of that date, when he gave a report of his world tour. He said this:
I want to assure hon. members that everywhere I went as a representative of Canada I was received with enthusiasm and every evidence of friendliness and good will. Everywhere I went I heard "O Canada" sung, and I was always moved and touched at the feeling of pride it gave one to be there as a representative of that country for which the hymn was being sung or played.
Consequently, Mr. Speaker, I wonder what right the ministers of the crown have to proclaim one national hymn instead of another, when this one hymn is recognized abroad.
I would now like, Mr. Speaker, to deal briefly with the comments made by the Minister of Defence Production (Mr. O'Hurley) which the hon. member for Hull (Mr. Caron) has mentioned during his remarks. I may say to the hon. minister that the Civil Service Commission is composed of honest and competent people, and that it is playing an important part in our administration. This commission has been founded so as to prevent the civil service from becoming chaotic and a political football, and so that government employees should enjoy security in their jobs as much as it is possible. During its 22 years in power, the Liberal government created a very competent Civil Service Commission which is admired in other countries. I consider that the commission which administers this institution should not become subject to politics and become the creature or the screen of a single party.

Today I want first of all
to speak about this beautiful county of Mon-treal-Laval which I have the honour to represent. I have, Mr. Speaker, the pleasure and honour to represent one of the most beautiful counties of the land, whatever my hon. fellow members may say, which is also one of the most densely populated areas of the country, with a population of almost 250,000, comprising about 80,000 voters. The county of Montreal-Laval is situated north of the city of Montreal. It also comprises Jesus island, bound on the north by the Thousand Islands river and on the south by the Prairie river. Jesus island, Mr. Speaker, which is about 20 miles long and about 10 miles wide, is composed of 17 islands and municipalities, and also includes 22 school boards.
I need not mention that every day I receive many requests particularly from the municipal councils of those cities and municipalities. Now, Mr. Speaker, I would like to talk about the postal system in our county of Laval and, more particularly, the postal system we have on Jesus island. As I said, Jesus island comprises 17 towns and municipalities which have to administer a population of more than 100,000 people. There are also several towns and municipalities that are grouped together for postal delivery. There are 7 towns: St. Frangois, St. Elzear, Ste. Rose, Fa-breville, Laval West, Ste. Dorothee, and Laval Islands. We have for instance towns like Laval des Rapides which, in 1951, had a population of about 3,000 and now has more than 15,000, but has not yet its own post office.
I hope, Mr. Speaker, that the Post Office Department will give serious consideration to the matter, so as to improve the postal system in the constituency of Laval. There are also in my beautiful constituency of Laval a good number of farmers; each year they have to face the same problems in connection with their agricultural products. Should it be possible to establish a seasonal tariff on farm products and even put an embargo on imported products, I am sure that would be of great help to the farmers, not only of the constituency of Laval, but of the whole of Canada.
There are also, Mr. Speaker, many railway crossings in my constituency. Each year, many accidents, often fatal, occur. Why? Because there are no fences nor traffic lights. The hon. Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees) will assuredly want to give very special attention to the need of my constituency,


and, in that connection, I am sure he will see to it that it gets the share to which it is entitled. I should now like to deal with a matter in which I am specially interested. I refer to the deepening of the channel in the Prairie and Thousand Islands rivers to facilitate the use of pleasure craft.
