These two rivers cross the constituency of Laval from end to end. If you go round Jesus island by boat, you will travel a distance of about 50 miles, and you will also note from 3,000 to 3,500 motorboats of all kinds. I believe that development of these two rivers for the benefit of pleasure boats only, has become absolutely necessary, and that, for several reasons. First of all, according to the Financial Post in 1957 the sale of pleasure boats in Canada alone increased by $30 million over the previous year. Think of the ever increasing number of pleasure boats, of the fact that these cruiser type boats are now within reach of anyone's purse, that the number of persons making a living out of the pleasure boating industry, and of the increased value it would mean for land adjacent to navigable rivers. Consider too that the navigable waterways of some lakes and rivers are the sole means of communication, and that over 90 per cent of riparian proprietors own some sort of boat. Do not forget the commercial expansion that navigation means for riparian proprietors, municipalities and cities; think of the tremendous development of aquatic sports, of their popularity, of the power and speed of outboard motors and yachts, and consider also, more especially, that our navigable waterways offer panoramic and tourist attractions unexplored until now, not to mention that, in case of emergency, navigable rivers are the only means of transportation. Let us consider too the expansion of industry, the success of enterprises and professions connected with it, such as insurance, sale of oil and gasoline, sale of boat, life saving and fire prevention equipment, of marine paints and varnishes, as well as boat and motor maintenance and repair services. Moreover, Mr. Speaker, in deepening these rivers it would make it possible to clean up their waters and would permit the development of beautiful beaches. Action on this highly important matter would benefit the entire population of the Laval constituency, which I am intent on helping.

Please be assured, Mr. Speaker, that the people place high hopes in the new administration to study and solve the many problems of my constituency.
Now, Mr. Speaker, may I say just a few words on unemployment.
Of course, some unemployment exists. It always has existed and always will.
In the constituency of Laval perhaps I am rather privileged, as this is a residential constituency and the majority of the people there are home owners so far and have not suffered too much from unemployment. However, I think it is important to prepare a broad plan providing for the construction of industrial and commercial buildings, and giving due consideration to available manpower in each section of the country. Under this plan, an attempt would be made to obtain advance information on the rate of construction in each area, and to ensure that at least 90 per cent of skilled workers were kept employed. An effort would be made to have new construction projects undertaken in all areas where a slowdown occurred.
I realize that the implementation of this plan would probably entail a great deal of work, but perhaps there might be created a new department, which might be called the Department of Town Planning, Construction and Housing, which would take in the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank the population of the constituency of Laval for their confidence and co-operation. In return, I promise them my best efforts on their behalf.

Mr. Speaker, it is a duty this year for all members of this house, to voice the opinions of their constituents, in view of the serious situation facing all constituencies throughout the country.
I have been listening with much pleasure to the hon. member for Laval (Mr. Bour-dages), making his maiden speech in this house. He did quite well, and I congratulate him on this first effort. I hope we shall be hearing more of him.
Mr. Speaker, may I, as did all previous speakers, congratulate the proposer and seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne (Messrs. Jorgenson and Fortin). I wish, particularly, to congratulate the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) who, in a speech that lasted over
The Address-Mr. Dupuis two hours, drew a true picture of conditions facing Canadians under a Conservative government.
I can recall how during the election campaigns of 1957 and 1958, our hon. friends across the room openly criticized the Liberal government and asked people to elect a Conservative government that promised heaven on earth.
Well, Mr. Speaker, the Conservative party has been in power only slightly over a year. In a matter of a few months, Mr. Speaker, we are back to the empty and dark years with which Conservative governments have always plagued this country throughout its history: the Borden government, the Bennett government, and now the Diefenbaker government.
Mr. Speaker, how often have we heard it said: "Beat the Liberals and there will be no unemployed in the country. Beat the Liberals and we will settle the problem of federal-provincial relations. Beat the Liberals, and Canada will enjoy prosperity such as it has never known." Since the beginning of this session, certain members of the right- who will come to the left very soon-have shouted at every turn, as do, for instance, the hon. members for Roberval (Mr. Tremblay), for Joliette - L'Assomption - Montcalm (Mr. Pigeon) and for Sherbrooke (Mr. Allard), who are all Union Nationale Conservatives from the province of Quebec, and who were elected because they promised in all ridings of the province of Quebec to lead Canada to the very peak of prosperity.
Mr. Speaker, I would prefer that, instead of interrupting the speeches of those who are discharging their duties, hon. members, and particularly the member for Roberval, described to their voters and to us the situation that existed when he won the riding in 1958, and of the situation in which the Conservative party has placed the same riding a few months after gaining power.
In regard to the Roberval constituency, for instance, this afternoon, I secured the latest statistics, and they are not at all pretty. In fact, I would be ashamed to rise in this parliament of Canada and to be part of the Conservative team that was so critical of the St. Laurent government, the government which led the country to the highest peak of achievement since confederation, and end up with the result that is experienced now since the professor of Laval University, a 100 per cent "duplessist" was elected to this house.

The Address-Mr. Dupuis
In the riding of my friend from Roberval, in May 1957, under the Liberal administration, there were 1,589 unemployed. A year after our friend's victory, in May 1958, in the same constituency of Roberval, under the leadership of the great and worthy new member, there were 3,794 unemployed, an increase of 2,205 in a year.
In June 1957, in the riding of Roberval, there were 1,186 unemployed, and since our friends took power, in June 1958, there were 2,713, an increase of 1,527 in a single year.
And, I look now at my friend from Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm (Mr. Pigeon) he of the serene smile, that ex-private secretary to the "duplessist" minister of labour

who also likes to sing the praises of the Conservative administration. Well, may I advise him to think of the change that can happen under a new government; I will give him the figures on his own constituency, the figures for "his village" as Mr. Duplessis would put it.
At Joliette, in May 1957, 1609 unemployed were registered at the unemployment insurance office; in May 1958, a year after the election of the devoted secretary to Mr. Duplessis' minister of labour, there were 3,410 unemployed receiving unemployment insurance benefits, an increase of 1,801.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to express my appreciation for this opportunity of taking part m the debate on the speech from the throne, and to bring up several matters of interest to my constituents. I should like to associate myself with those other hon. members who have congratulated the mover (Mr. Jorgenson) and seconder (Mr. Fortin) of the address in reply. Their speeches did credit to themselves and credit to this house. I feel the opposition should also be congratulated on the enthusiasm and even the fervour with which they carried on their duty of criticism, especially in view of the fact that they have such a weak case on which to work. As is customary in throne speech debates the opposition has seen fit to move an amendment which implies want of confidence in the government. I, of course, along with my colleagues am very much opposed to any such amendment. We feel the government has done a good job and we wish to congratulate all concerned on their administration.
While the effects of government policy bear unequally on different groups in our economy the overall results of these policies have, we believe, been good for Middlesex West and good for Canada. All government is a compromise. In our intricate present day society when one group is helped another group may be hurt. We cannot all benefit equally through government policies all of the time. Equity is an ideal that we have to strive for but which we have no hope of attaining.

Care must be exercised by government to promote equity. We believe our government has exercised such care.
All of us when considering economic propositions must remember to consider what their future effects will be as well as the present advantages of such propositions. For instance, it is folly to set farm prices at a level which will produce unmanageable surpluses. It is folly also to set up unemployment insurance plans that defeat themselves by destroying the incentive of people to work. Constant increases in wages and prices can only result in ever increasing spirals of inflation and end in financial disaster. We must remember that every time we increase our social security we must sacrifice a corresponding part of our individual freedom in the spending of our income. As a people we must give if we are to get. We cannot take from our national pool of wealth more than we put in. We submit that the caution with which our government has moved in the exercise of its functions has inspired confidence among people everywhere.
I have great faith in our Canadian people. We will stand together to maintain Canada as the best country in the world in which to live. In 1957 Canadians chose a new government which they believed would best serve Canada's needs. In 1958 they confirmed that choice by returning the government to office with the greatest majority ever given a government in this country. There are no grounds for belief that the confidence of the people in our government has weakened in the slightest degree.
Federal-provincial relationships have improved since this government took office. Never before has this country been so united as it is today. Commonwealth bonds have been strengthened by the commonwealth conference held last year and by the Prime Minister's recent visit to commonwealth countries. Our Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) and our government have clearly demonstrated their dedication to the cause of commonwealth development and their belief in the great role which the British commonwealth can play in world affairs.
Our good relationships with the United States have been maintained and improved. Our interests have been stated frankly and frankly discussed. A greater measure of mutual respect and trust has been the result. Our interests in trade and defence are so closely bound to those of our southern neighbours that the best and most cordial relationship with them are essential for our mutual benefit.
The constituency of Middlesex West, which I have the honour to represent, is a representative Canadian riding. It is both urban

and rural, industrial and agricultural. Although we are an inland area the great lakes are near enough that the future of the St. Lawrence seaway has a very significant place in our future plans. Our constituency is characterized by numerous new suburban homes, light industry and diversified agriculture. Our factories make aluminum products, tubular fittings, plumbing and heating supplies, woollen goods, furniture, drainage tile, agricultural chemicals, mobile homes and store equipment. We have plants which process meat products, poultry products, dairy products, fruits and vegetables and also plants which mill flour and feed. Our farmers produce in some quantity nearly every product of agriculture that can be produced in any part of Canada: grain and seeds, fruits and vegetables, every kind of livestock and tobacco. From our woodlots come Christmas trees and large quantities of hardwood for manufacturing.
We have ethnic problems similar to those in some other parts of the country. The first settlers in Middlesex West were almost exclusively of British descent; English, Irish, Welsh and Scottish. In recent years the character of the population has changed and in some areas nearly half the population now are new Canadians. Because we are both urban and rural, industrial and agricultural, owners and wage earners, importers and exporters, old Canadians and new Canadians, debtors and creditors, we find ourselves on both sides of nearly every social and economic argument that is taking place in Canada today.
Middlesex West welcomes the announcement that a visit to the city of London is to be included in the royal tour this summer. Since our constituency includes the western suburb of the city this announcement is of special significance to us. Our people greatly appreciate this honour and I am sure will cooperate in every possible way to prepare a royal welcome.
We are thankful to be able to say that unemployment in our area is not as serious as in some other places but we have it. Our people endorse the various policies of the government aimed at easing its effects. The extension of seasonal benefits under the unemployment insurance plan and the removal of all restrictions in connection with federal sharing of direct relief costs has been of great assistance. The government's public works program of construction, and the encouragement of special municipal programs of winter work by a federal grant of 75 per cent of the labour costs should also help to provide jobs. I am glad to see that a new central school is to be constructed by the Indian affairs branch on this reservation. I wish to commend the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mrs. Fairclough) for this action and to express to her the appreciation of our people that it has been found possible to increase the educational facilities here. I have had the privilege of visiting several of the classrooms on the reserve and watching the pupils at work and I would say, judging from what I saw, that those boys and girls on the reserve will make the best possible use of the new facilities. I have been assured that the facilities provided will be of the highest standard. I am glad of that assurance because those people deserve the best. As their representative it is a part of my responsibility to see that they get the best.
The most noticeable feature of the reserve that strikes one when driving through it is the growth of weeds and brush everywhere in evidence. This reserve has in it some very fine agricultural land. I feel that it should not be lying idle and growing up to weeds. In bygone years this land was used for growing crops, but of late years agricultural activities on the reserve have been curtailed. There are a number of reasons why this has happened.
Most reserve land is divided into small farms of fewer than 50 acres; parts of these farms have never been cultivated, so that the fields that once were cultivated would range in size from 2 to 20 acres. There are


some large fields and some large farms on the reserve that are farmed with power machinery but small farmers cannot afford modern equipment with which to carry on their agriculture, and so the fields have been abandoned and are growing up to weeds and brush.
Another reason for the abandonment of those fields is the lack of tile drainage. When horse power was used drainage was not so essential. Horses do not get stuck in mud-holes as tractors do. In our constituency tile drainage is essential for farming with power equipment. There is little hope of reviving agricultural activities on this reserve without more tile drainage. Our Indians have requested assistance in reviving agriculture on their reserve. On their behalf, therefore, I request that the government give consideration to having a tile drainage plan prepared for this reserve and that tile drainage work be undertaken.
To prevent a further deterioration of reserve land and to make it possible for small land owners to use their land to advantage while still holding jobs in industry, or after retirement, I request that farm equipment, together with trained operators, be made available on a custom work basis for the use of small land owners on the reserve.
The people of Middlesex West are seriously disturbed about the ever increasing power of labour bosses and their ability to paralyse our economy with strikes. Our people feel that the time has come when serious consideration should be given to the provision of safeguards against the abuse of union power. This suggestion implies no hostility whatsoever to the legitimate aims of labour unions.
Not only does this uneasiness prevail among non-union people but in the ranks of organized labour as well. Much is read and heard these days of the unscrupulous conduct of some labour leaders, and the seeming inability or lack of desire on the part of the unions to control or replace them. One explanation is that the rank and file of the membership in some unions have lost control through lack of interest and nonattendance at meetings and a situation develops where control cannot be regained. There are stories of hoodlum tactics being used by labour bosses to retain their power when criticism of them within a union develops.
Regardless of how their control came about, the hard fact remains that labour bosses are in a position to impose their will on essential parts of our economy. Our people feel that this should not be. We have legislation to curb improper exploitation of the public by

big business and many believe the time has come when serious consideration should be given to the imposition of safeguards against unscrupulous abuses of power by big labour.
Now that labour unions have become so powerful that they can impose their will on the country by strikes or threatened strikes which would paralyse our economy by tying up transportation or cutting off essential supplies such as fuel or electricity, without which many communities could not survive, our people say that it is time to take remedial action before the situation gets out of hand.
Labour unions were organized originally to raise the wages and improve the working conditions of the low-paid workers in industry. The trend now is to help the highest paid workers to get more. Today big labour is being used to boost ever higher and higher the wages of those already at the top of the labour scale. We are building up in this country a high-cost economy which constantly increases our difficulty in competing for world markets. We are pricing ourselves out of business. Our people feel that this problem of high-cost production must be faced and steps taken to prevent our economy getting further out of line with world markets.
The ability of big labour to dictate ever higher wages in the industries under their control is creating unrest among all groups in our society and is one of the principal contributing factors to inflation. Earners of smaller wages and salaries in industry, agriculture and the professions are demanding that they be kept in line with labour on a percentage basis. This constant pressure on the wage and salary line, this "keeping up with the Joneses" in industry is probably one of the main factors in increasing costs.
Labour is not alone to blame for our present economic instability. It is a trend of the times. Everybody is out for himself; everybody wants more. What makes big labour show up so boldly in this mad race is that they have the inside of the track and are taking full advantage of it. Some day, somehow, this mad race must end. Our people are looking hopefully to the government to provide the incentive which is necessary and which only the government has the strength to provide to guide our economy into a more stable condition. Our people believe that one incentive to stability would be to restore the control of labour unions to the rank and file of the membership and to curb the ever-increasing power of the labour bosses.
Our people will expect the government to give the most careful consideration to the
66968-9-15J
The Address-Mr. Thomas recent civil service commission recommendation that certain collective bargaining privileges be extended to civil servants. This is a new departure in Canada and requires most careful consideration on the part of all concerned. Such action might ultimately lead to the unionization of the civil service under foreign labour control. We believe that such a development would be most undesirable.
Middlesex West was endowed by nature with some of the finest agricultural land to be found in Canada. We can grow everything that will grow in any part of the country. Our agricultural products are much diversified. Some of our farmers are still labouring under the effects of an adverse cost-price squeeze but others have enjoyed a good measure of prosperity in 1958. It depends on the line of production in which they are engaged. Crops this year were good. We had record yields of grain and apples. Higher prices for cattle in 1958 have given many of our farmers a great lift.
Our wheat producers took an active part in organizing the Ontario wheat marketing board. This board got into operation just as harvesting began in 1958 and some difficulties were experienced in handling the first of the crop. As time goes on, however, the difficulties are being ironed out and this wheat marketing board should prove of great benefit to Ontario wheat producers by helping to stabilize the price. The departments of agriculture and trade and commerce have assisted in the solution of some of these Ontario wheat problems.
Ontario corn producers have been working for some months to establish a corn marketing board. We wish them success in their efforts. They have requested that corn be designated a commodity for support under the Agricultural Prices Support Act but we regret that so far no satisfactory formula for supporting corn has been found. Negotiations are still continuing.
Comments have been made in this debate about the improvement in our adverse balance of trade. We have a suggestion to make in this regard. Normally large quantities of soya beans are imported into this country. We use about 15 million bushels per year and we grow about half of our requirements. We are quite capable of producing all of our requirements of soya beans and we believe that it would be good business to encourage our farmers to increase their production.
We request that consideration be given to increasing the support price on soya beans to encourage greater production. In addition to improving our foreign trade deficit by cutting down our imports, we would take

The Address-Mr. Thomas acreage out of the production of surplus commodities such as wheat. Soya bean growers are irked because there is a $1.20 per bushel tariff against our soya beans going into the United States but United States soya beans enter Canada free. Our producers would welcome some adjustment to decrease this discrepancy.
The program of price supports under the Agricultural Prices Support Act has operated with reasonable satisfaction in our area. While our agricultural producers have argued for higher support prices, they appreciate the caution of the government and the board in setting prices. Our people agree that it is better to start low and make increases where necessary than to start too high and get into trouble with unmanageable surpluses. We subscribe to the theory that the law of supply and demand will ultimately prevail, and that while temporary support prices may be desirable to soften the efforts of sudden and drastic market changes, price supports should not be considered as permanent fixtures in regard to any commodity.
We feel that the best and soundest method of obtaining fair prices for agricultural products is the organization by the farmers themselves of commodity marketing boards and that such boards should accept the responsibility for adjusting production to market requirements.
We welcome the announcement in the speech from the throne that our present farm credit facilities are to be reviewed with the object of making it possible for farmers to obtain financial assistance in modernizing their operations. Improved credit facilities should go a long way in helping farmers out of the present cost-price squeeze by providing for necessary expansion of operation and the installation of labour saving equipment.
Again we wish to urge upon the government the advisability of bringing farm labour under the provisions of the Unemployment Insurance Act. Farmers are finding it ever more difficult to get help. People tend to avoid farm jobs because they get no unemployment insurance credits. Farmers are having trouble enough in competing for labour because of high industrial wage rates. They should not be further handicapped by lack of unemployment insurance coverage. We request that the government give further consideration to this matter.
We welcome the statement in the speech from the throne that the humane slaughter bill is to be referred to the agriculture committee. It is our opinion that the agricultural representatives in the house, who are most closely associated with the production and

care of farm animals, would appreciate most keenly the necessity for promoting humane methods of slaughter.
A matter of immediate concern to our people is the extension of the current rabies epidemic into Middlesex county. Animals in several parts of the county have been diagnosed as rabid and several people have taken anti-rabies treatments. On January 6 the agriculture committee of the Middlesex county council called a meeting of county officials, federal and provincial members of parliament, health officials, conservation officers and others to discuss the situation. A resolution was passed asking that clinics be established to immunize pet animals as a safeguard against the infection of humans. We were informed by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Harkness) by telegram on January 8 that the rabies situation in Middlesex county was being closely watched, that a survey of the county would be made but that present commitments prevented the immediate establishment of inoculation clinics.
A story has been circulating in our area that no more heads of animals are to be sent to the Hull laboratory for examination unless human beings have been exposed. At the same time the story states that until there is more evidence of an increase in the incidence of the disease, clinics will not be established. Our people are wondering how we are to find out whether the disease is increasing when no more heads of animals are to be examined.
I have been informed by departmental officials and by the minister that the intentions of the health of animals branch are very much misunderstood in this regard. In areas such as Middlesex West where the disease has only recently made its appearance the laboratory is examining as many heads as they can get in order to keep track of developments. But in areas such as Grey county and the counties in the northern part of the province where the disease has been established for a considerable time and has probably reached a maximum of intensity, it is a waste of time to continue to examine animal heads unless for a specific purpose such as to determine whether or not a person has been exposed to infection by a rabid animal.
Our health officials favour setting up the clinics at the time when they are most likely to exert the maximum deterrent effect on the spread of the disease. They are watching Middlesex county closely with this fact in mind and as soon as the time is ripe for action clinics will be established.
We have a woollen industry in our constituency. It is not a large industry, but it

is important to many of our people. This industry is having serious difficulty in meeting the competition of imported goods from low cost countries. They contend that tariff protection alone cannot solve their problem. They request control of imports by quota so that a fair share of the Canadian market may be retained for Canadian manufacturers.
Because of the relative size of the markets in the United States as compared to the size of the markets in Canada, the unit cost of tooling up for production is lower in the United States than it is in Canada. Our manufacturing industry needs protection because of this and probably will continue to need protection for a long time to come. Some Canadian industries, such as the farm implement companies, may have grown to a size where their volume permits them to compete on equal terms with United States industry, but this is generally not the case. Our smaller industries especially are in need of special consideration if Canadian industry as a whole is to survive and prosper.
I wish to express our appreciation to the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. MacLean) for a very interesting and educational tour with him through the fisheries research laboratory in London. I was much surprised at the magnitude of its operation. This laboratory carries on the departmental research program for all fresh water fisheries in Canada. We of Middlesex West appreciate the location of this fine institution in our area.
The new national hospitalization plan, as it applies in Ontario since January 1 of this year, has been well received. More than 91 per cent of the people of Ontario are now covered. This exceeds expectations. Individuals are included in the plan on a voluntary basis, and people have signed up faster than was expected. This is a good indication that the plan fills a need in our economy. The plan will assist municipalities by eliminating much of the need for indigent hospital care. Because the plan permits hospitals to increase their rates to cover costs, hospital deficits which municipalities have been compelled to carry heretofore should disappear. Relief from this indigent hospital care and these hospital deficits should provide substantial assistance in the preparation of municipal budgets. Our government is entitled to much credit for speeding up the establishment of this new social service.
Nothing in the government's record of accomplishments since they took office has brought more satisfaction to our people than the administration of the Department of Veterans Affairs. The people of Middlesex West, together with the people in all parts of
The Address-Mr. A. Brassard Canada, will stand firmly behind the government in providing a fair deal for our veterans. All proposals and recommendations made by the Canadian Legion for improving the legislation and regulations in connection with veterans affairs have been given sympathetic consideration and, when possible, put into effect.
I have heard much recently about repeal of section 34 of the Combines Investigation Act. I believe that this proposal involves fundamental rights of individuals as well as fundamental rights of the public. Before a decision is made I would suggest that this matter be referred to a competent independent tribunal for investigation and recommendation.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, may I say that the record of our government and the confidence which they enjoy amongst the people in all parts of Canada, constitutes abundant reason why these amendments now before us should be voted down.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we usually see in the chair the Speaker of this house and we take pleasure in telling him how we appreciate his work among us. Tonight I am happy to see the Acting Speaker occupy the chair as this gives me the opportunity to pay him a tribute for his sense of fairness and also for his sense of humour, although the occasion to show the latter seldom arises.
I would beg the Acting Speaker to be kind enough to convey to the Speaker the following message. I too have great pleasure in seeing again this year the Speaker of the house preside over the sometimes stormy proceedings of this assembly. Even though we are all aware that in view of the deeply human phase of his training, his extensive knowledge and his culture he is destined to still higher functions, if possible, we will be sorry to see the day when we are deprived of the pleasure of appreciating daily his sense of fairness and also, as in your case, Mr. Acting Speaker, his sense of humour which makes things so much easier in the heat of the debates.
Like the previous speakers, I congratulate the movers of the address in reply to the speech from the throne (Mr. Jorgenson and Mr. Fortin).
Both were a credit to their party and to their constituencies by the way in which they fulfilled the difficult and challenging task given to them by the right hon. Prime Minister of this country (Mr. Diefenbaker).

The Address-Mr. A. Brassard
I will no doubt have the indulgence of the house if I am a bit more personal in my remarks in regard to the hon. member for Montmagny-L'Islet, not because I failed to convince his constituents to elect another representative, not because he tried himself to convince my constituents that they should vote for someone else, but rather because I have known him since my college years, as well as several members of his family.
Let me say that his distinguished brother Andre and I were fellow students. This brother is now a Catholic chaplain with our army. I also know other members of his family, and I can say with every sincerity and honesty that every one of them is a credit to their distinguished parents.
However, I would not want the hon. member for Montmagny-L'Islet to infer from these remarks that I wholly endorse the actions and policies of the new Conservative government of Canada.
Mr. Speaker, first I wish to thank the Conservative government for having provided this house with simultaneous translation. I do not believe that there is anything humiliating nor degrading for any one to recognize the good one finds in his opponent, and it is for this reason that I will rather speak in French, thus breaking away from a tradition which I used to observe, that is to speak at least fifteen minutes in English and fifteen minutes in French when delivering a speech in this house.
Mr. Speaker, what I should like to establish in my speech, is that there is a lack of cohesion among the ministers who lay down the general policy or administer our national affairs.
Let us examine for instance the field of agriculture, for one. I do not need to remind the hon. members that the hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Harkness) who, fortunately, is in his seat tonight, addressed the Saskatchewan Farmers' Union not so long ago. He then expressed before the members of that group his personal ideas on agriculture in our country. The press made much of his speech and did not fail to recall what the right hon. Prime Minister had said on the same subject on another occasion. If the house will permit I will quote the Western Producer of December 18, 1958 in order to show to what extent the Minister of Agriculture and the right hon. Prime Minister are in perfect agreement on Canadian agricultural policy. I will put on the record part of the report in the Western Producer of December 18, 1958. I quote:

(Text):
In his address to the annual convention of the Saskatchewan Farmers Union Mr. Harkness, the Minister of Agriculture, touched on the question of reducing production. He was throwing out a strong hint when he said: "I feel that some voluntary reduction of wheat acreage in favour of diversification should be undertaken to relieve congestion in the wheat trade." Arguing in favour of this suggestion he went on to state: "In these days of a semi-controlled economy it seems natural to suggest that control be exercised at the producing level as well as at the marketing level, for it is at the production level that alternatives exist."
Mr. Harkness has been giving air to these similar sentiments off and on for some time. It is no exaggeration on our part when we say that we see in this an appalling state of affairs. It indicates a total lack of understanding of world conditions as they exist now. This in a minister of the crown, a leading member of the Diefenbaker cabinet, is a very serious matter.
One wonders whether Mr. Harkness realizes that he is taking direct issue with his own leader when he proposes restricting production? Perhaps it will refresh his memory if we quote again the remarks made by Mr. Diefenbaker when he opened the Saskatoon exhibition after his first victory at the polls last year. The new Prime Minister then said:
"To those who think that in agriculture we have arrived at a point where we need no longer expand I say to you this:"-
And you know, Mr. Speaker, that the Prime Minister is a very good orator.
"-I learned one lesson at the commonwealth conference in London. We must expand our agricultural development.
With one quarter of the world's population going to bed hungry at night methods must be found to enable the distribution of our surpluses to the end that happiness will come to the peoples of the world.
"Together we must preserve the peace of the world and hold ourselves through agriculture as a bulwark against communism."
Who speaks for the government, Mr. Harkness arguing for restriction or Mr. Diefenbaker advocating expansion?-
Yet Mr. Harkness talks of restriction. Let him read these further words of his leader. Speaking in New York on the eve of his departure on his world tour Mr. Diefenbaker said:
"The great triangle of nations-Great Britain, the United States and Canada-must join with others of like mind in a common effort to assure new hope for the betterment of peoples who have been disfranchised from the bounties of providence.
"It is a primary duty to be our brother's keeper to those underdeveloped areas of the world and to give aid, both economic and technical, so that the gulf between their living standards and ours shall become narrower.
"Since we in North America are blest with more than our share of the good things of life we have an overriding mandate m that we must help those who have less."-
And Mr. Harkness wants to reduce production! How can he win with plenty if he deliberately promotes scarcity? How can he eradicate want in needy countries unless he can devise acceptable methods of distributing food to those who haven't ready cash? Mr. Harkness and his colleagues have a lot to learn before they catch up with and fully understand the policies enunciated by their leader.

The Address-Mr. A. Brassard
(Translation):
Mr. Speaker, we fully support the policy advocated by the right hon. Prime Minister when he said he wanted to assist underdeveloped countries where people by the thousands die of starvation. I wonder however, if we will ever hear in this house some members from the province of Quebec- and I say this without bias or malice-speak in support of this policy of assisting within our means the underdeveloped countries.
In the province of Quebec there are many people-I will not mention any of them- who speak against communism. In my opinion, one of the most effective measures to fight communism is to close the door to communist countries with regard to their possible influence in the countries which are not yet open to that influence.
I hope that the members from the province of Quebec who will speak after us in this debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne will clearly express their views on the matter.
May I be allowed also to say a few words about dominion-provincial relations. I followed quite closely, and you will easily understand why, Mr. Speaker, the electoral campaign of 1957. Shortly after the people of Canada had clearly expressed their opinion about the government they wanted, an outstanding member of the Liberal party compiled the promises made by the right hon. Prime Minister throughout the country when he was touring the ten provinces to canvass for the votes of the Canadians at the election of June 10. He spoke with eloquence-everybody knows it-in the ten provinces of this country. He dealt with every subject. He committed himself. He committed himself, I repeat, in many fields. He staked his name. He even committed the future Prime Minister of this country-of course he did not know at the time who it would be, otherwise he would not have spoken so much. He committed the future Prime Minister of this country in many fields of politics. He spoke especially and repeatedly about dominion-provincial relations.
I should like to quote, for instance, what he said in April 1957-on the 25th to be more precise-in Toronto. His speech was published in the Montreal Star of April 26, 1957. According to the Montreal Star he said:
(Text):
There could not be national unity if the provinces were handcuffed by inadequate sources of revenue, with several of the provinces unable to discharge their constitutional responsibilities and promote the development of natural resources. A Conservative-organized dominion-provincial conference would settle this problem in a spirit of unity, amity, and with good will, tolerance and respect.
(Translation):
He has travelled throughout the country. His colleagues have also travelled in many provinces assuring that if a Conservative government came into power, the matter of federal-provincial relations would be settled once and for all. What happened after the elections? I must admit that a federal-provincial conference was convened. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) was there; I don't know whether he was tired, but he was there. The Prime Minister was there. They listened to the claims of the various provinces and what did the Minister of Finance have to say after hearing the claims of premiers. He said: You ask an enormous increase in the amount you are getting. You are to go back home, we are going to study your suggestions, and we shall call another federal-provincial conference for the beginning of 1958.
What happened. Oh, in the very first months of 1958, the Minister of Finance sent a telegram to all provincial treasurers, outlining the terms offered by the federal government to the provinces regarding fiscal matters. There has been no other federal-provincial conference, yet the Minister of Finance had definitely promised that there would be another one at the beginning of
1958.	The Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister, as well as all their colleagues, were secretly plotting something else. They were plotting another election.
I am not blaming them because they did not have a sufficient majority to speak with authority in the house. But why not say so to the people, why make promises when you know beforehand that you cannot fulfill them? I realize that the Conservative government was not able to keep its promises. What I do not understand as easily is that at the present time, it does not even think of convening the representatives of the provinces to discuss fiscal problems. It could also take this opportunity to discuss unemployment.
The speech from the throne dashed all our hopes in that respect. The provinces were asked to show understanding in fiscal matters. The Prime Minister informed us that he had written to the provincial premiers to tell them that they had to co-operate in the study of that problem. Such a request is contained in the last speech from the throne. And I am positive that there will be legislation laid before the house to ask us to approve of the ideas of the cabinet concerning the extension for a further year of the dominion-provincial agreements. But why doesn't the cabinet or

The Address-Mr. A. Brassard the government simply tell us the plain truth about it? They do not specify why they do not intend to call a meeting of representatives of the provinces in Ottawa this year. And if the Prime Minister intends to call such a meeting, being so jealous personally of the prerogatives and rights of parliament in every field, why does he not say so? It is a fact that the Prime Minister, with his strong voice, his gestures and his personality, has convinced the Canadian people that the Liberal government had not done justice to the opposition when the Conservatives were sitting on this side. Why does the Conservative government not give the example today by saying why it has no intention of asking provincial governments to examine our problems? He could also call a conference to look into the matter of unemployment. I do not wish to play politics with unemployment. Too many members in this house use this calamity to play politics.
Mr. Speaker, I hear our hon. opponents applaud my statement that too many members in the house try to play politics with unemployment. I believe-and you can applaud again-I believe that we should consider the question of unemployment from a human point of view and try to find a solution.
I listened very carefully to the hon. Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) when he spoke today. He is a man I admire and for whom I have great regard. He tries to consider the problem and find a solution, but at the same time he blames the opposition for not offering any suggestion. But, is the Conservative cabinet made up of a group of ministers who work only on suggestions from the opposition? They are there precisely to work and to find solutions. The Diefenbaker cabinet is responsible for the administration of our country's affairs. They are the ones who went to the people and said: "We have problems in this country; you elect us and we shall solve them". Once in office, the Conservatives want the opposition to find every solution for them. To be honest I must say that the Minister of Labour and a few of his colleagues did try in vain to find solutions, but they did not solve the problem. Unemployment is still here and I believe we should find a solution to the unemployment situation in Canada. There is such a thing as the dominion bureau of statistics, the D.B.S. There is a big difference between figures released by the D.B.S. and those provided by employment offices throughout the country. I know from experience-I have never been Minister of Labour and I shall never be,

thank heaven for our people-but I know from experience that the Minister of Labour is in possession of statistics which are much higher than those given by the dominion bureau of statistics. I was a civil servant before becoming a lowly member of parliament, and I know that those statistics are much more alarming than those published by the dominion bureau of statistics. I shall not quote any figure, though the figure is known to me. But when one looks at the number of persons without jobs or looking for one throughout the country, it is something appalling, something pitiful. There are not only people seekings jobs, not only thousands of people receiving unemployment insurance benefits, not to mention the few thousands who are not even receiving such benefits, but there are all those who are depending on their father or mother, and who are receiving absolutely nothing. At this stage, I might as well add a word about my constituency. The Aluminum Company of Canada, whose main plant is in Arvida, has twice reduced its working staff by 10 per cent. There are also, in my constituency, two mills operated by Price Brothers. They have now reduced the work week to between 24 and 32 hours.
Those are the only two basic industries in the constituency of Lapointe. We have lost part of the British market and part of the French market for aluminum. England, which I deeply respect as a country, is the mother country of a great number of my fellow-citizens as France is the mother country of a great number of my fellow-citizens too. England is part of the commonwealth, but it buys part of its aluminum from Russia, which doubtlessly is also part of the commonwealth of nations. I find this situation painful. I am all for helping our two mother countries, France and England. We are making sacrifices to help other nations in many fields, and I would mention NATO as only one example. But why, when the time comes to reciprocate, why is no consideration given to the sacrifices we have made?
Mr. Speaker, having been myself a civil servant under the former Liberal administration-it is perhaps for that reason that we were defeated-I am fully aware of the sacrifices that Canada has made for England and France. As I said a moment ago, these two countries are our mother countries, and I know that we must help them. But why do they not take into account what we have done for them? If cuts in personnel had to be made in the Arvida aluminum company, I think it is due to the fact that we have lost a great part of our external trade with the English and the French.

The same situation obtains with regard to paper. We used to sell much of our paper to the United States, but thanks to the very friendly policy of the Conservatives towards the United States, we lost a part of our U.S. paper market.
Mr. Speaker, the Conservatives are logical people-I do not ask you to applaud, because you will be disappointed if you do- they are a tremendously logical lot!
In the field of trade, for instance-and I said it here myself last year-in the course of the last election campaign, the Conservatives, led by the Prime Minister, kicked the American government-and I hope that this time the Canadian Press will not mistranslate words.
What have the Conservatives done in the field of defence? After kicking Americans in the pants, they kissed them on both cheeks. They entrusted to an American citizen the integrated defence of Canada and the United States. I am not criticizing the fact that we have entrusted our integrated defence to General Partridge. I am only blaming the inconsistency of their conduct. In the field of trade, we kick them in the pants and in the field of defence we kiss them on both cheeks. That is a typical example of the tremendous logic of the Conservative government which is governing or perhaps I should say ruling us at this time.
Not only in this field have the Conservatives given us a truly magnificent show of consistency. You will recall, Mr. Speaker, the speeches made in 1957 by the right hon. Prime Minister and by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Pearkes). I note that the latter is now using his interpretation earphone. You will recall that the Minister of National Defence promised to cut down the defence appropriation by $500 million. That department, in his view, was running into staggering expenditures that were not justified. That was his position before the elections. What happened after June 10? There was a conference in London, and my hon. friend the Minister of National Defence attended	this	conference	with	the PrimeMinister.	No	sooner	had	he	returned toOttawa than	press	reporters,	who quitenaturally	are	always on	the	look-out for
news, hastened to query our distinguished Minister of National Defence. He was asked then if he intended to implement the promise that was made of reducing defence ex-66968-9-16
The Address-Mr. Slogan penditures by $500 million. The minister, who was arriving from London, replied that this was impossible. He excused himself on the grounds that the blame must always be put on the Liberals-that he never had enough information when he sat on this side of the house and that the promise that had been made was due in part-he did not use the word ignorance, but it looked like that-to a lack of information. Consequently, taxes were reduced by $225 million, instead of the promised $500 million.
Mr. Speaker, it is by making promises of this kind to the people, and by not implementing them, that one convinces people that politicians are all birds of a feather, whether they are "blue" or "red", that they are men who say one thing during the election campaign and who act differently once they sit on the government side.
I wanted to direct some remarks to another hon. gentleman but, unfortunately, he is not here at the moment. I refer to the Postmaster General (Mr. Hamilton). Before I became a member of parliament, as I was saying, Mr. Speaker, I used to sit-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with a profound feeling of humility that I take my seat in the House of Commons. I have hardly thawed out as yet from the deep freeze by-election. I am rising in this great council of Canada for the first time and I should like to extend to you, sir, and to all members in this house the sincere best wishes and greetings of all the people of Springfield. You, sir, execute your duties in that manner of impartiality and restraint that adds dignity to your high office and inspires respect from both sides of this house.
I should also like to express my sincere congratulations to the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Jorgenson); my neighbouring constituency; and to my neighbour in the house, the hon. member for Montmagny-L'lslet (Mr. Fortin). Both of these hon. gentlemen made masterly speeches in moving and seconding the motion for an address in reply to the speech from the throne. I should also like to extend my congratulations to the hon. member for Grenville-Dundas (Mrs. Cassel-man) and to the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Hellyer) on their victories.
I should also like to join with the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Mandziuk), who

The Address-Mr. Slogan drew to the attention of the house today the fact that this is the fortieth anniversary of the declaration of independence by the Ukraine. As you know, sir, my forebears came from that country and it is indeed fitting that I should make my debut in the house on this day.
I am here only as the medium through which the people of Springfield expressed their confidence in our great leader, the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) and in the policies which this government has implemented, especially the agricultural policies. Therefore, I should like to express my gratitude to the people of Springfield for placing their trust in this government. Those people of all nationalities, religions, political affiliations and stations in life now place their faith in me to present their cause in this house and to offer leadership on their behalf. My only hope is that both in and out of this house I may justify that trust and earn that respect that is accorded to all members of parliament who dedicate themselves humbly and sincerely to the service of the principles of democracy.
In those principles we have a rich heritage. It took men of vision, courage and conviction to crystallize that heritage; it took statesmanship, diplomacy, and years of struggle. By that struggle our fathers of confederation conceived a new nation, uniting two languages and two creeds, and dedicated to the principles of unity, equality, opportunity and freedom. Today the familiar words of those men and of those who passed before them and their deeds are seldom heard and even less appreciated.
Springfield is a relatively new constituency, Mr. Speaker, having been created in 1914 and altered in 1924. It boasted only one Conservative representative in its history, Tom Hay, who was first elected in 1925, until our late member, Val Yacula, won it in 1958. Mr. Yacula was a quiet man who did a good job. In his memory I wish merely to quote a few words by Lord Baldwin:
A few years, and the voices of those addressing the house today will be silent, too. A few more years and their voices will be forgotten. But the character and the spirit remain to fortify the coming generations and to illuminate their paths.
I am proud to represent Springfield, because Springfield is a large, diversified and cosmopolitan constituency. Our people range from native Indians and metis, to the descendants of the Selkirk settlers. But the
majority are the colourful people of European descent who colonized the area at the turn of the century. I say "colonized" deliberately, because still today we have villages that are distinctly Ukrainian, Polish, French and German and others. Today, as time marches on and new generations are conceived, there is emerging by interaction and intermarriage that brand of distinct Canadianism, tolerant and stable of character, of which we are all so proud, each with a different and distinct background, each with a common dedication of loyalty and devotion to this country.
As I pass among the pioneers of Springfield, I see that time takes its toll. I see less and less of those gnarled hands, those deeply etched faces, those stooped backs of those hardy people, often illiterate, who were dumped off the C.P.R. at East Selkirk in their sheepskin coats, with nothing but their love of the land and enthusiasm for hard work. They did not think of themselves; they thought of the future. They were not ambitious for themselves but for the future generations. They carved a civilization out of the wilderness. But, more important still, they carved their brand, that sterling character of pioneering Canadianism that was instilled in their children and has carried them to respected positions of leadership on the broad frontiers of the world today. That inherent quality is emerging from an amorphous mass and crystallizing into a distinct Canadianism. I hope, Mr. Speaker, that those pious pioneers will find in their afterlife the peace and rewards that were never theirs on earth.
Springfield stretches from the metropolis of Winnipeg to the barren and inaccessible expanse of the pre-Cambrian shield in the north. In the bosom of these rocks lies the great wealth of gold, chrome, beryllium, nickel and other metals. We in Springfield share the vision of the north. We have placed our faith in men like our Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Hamilton), a hard-working minister whose efforts are often unrecognized and even less appreciated. At Bissett we have a thriving gold-mining community. In those northern areas there are also many trappers. Along lake Winnipeg we have a large commercial fishing industry which is being faced with grave and trying times by conditions in the lake and problems of marketing. I am

sure all hon. members know of and have tasted the famous lake Winnipeg goldeye.
At Victoria Beach and Bird's Hill and at other areas we have a multi-million dollar mink-farming industry. At Pine Falls we have a pulp and paper industry which employs 550 people and whose payroll is $2,500,000 annually. Nearly all the power generated in Manitoba is generated within Springfield along the Winnipeg river. At the present time we are constructing a great steam power plant in the town of East Selkirk, which will be converted to an atomic power plant as soon as it is feasible. We have at Lac Du Bonnet, our gateway to the north, an aeroplane and seaplane base. This town has an annual retail sales turnover of over $2 million. It has seven small industries in its vicinity, including the wild rice industry and granite quarries. We have the famous limestone quarries at Tyndall and Garson. Just east of these towns we have Beause-jour, which is the principal town in the constituency.
At Molson we have a big peat moss industry. In Springfield lies a great part of Manitoba's playgrounds. At Grand Beach we have beautiful white sand hills and in the Whiteshell area we have numerous resorts. We have hundreds of lakes and streams where sportsmen can enjoy the thrill of game fish and there is good hunting in our forests. We have a large oil refinery at East St. Paul, and we have numerous small industries and businesses.
But the welfare of Springfield as a whole depends upon agriculture. We have market gardening, mixed farming and grain growing, and the problems of agriculture are particularly pressing in my constituency because the farms are relatively small and therefore the cost-price squeeze bears more heavily upon us.
May I say that now we are going through the throes of an agricultural revolution very similar to the industrial revolution that other countries went through earlier. We appreciate the actions of the government with regard to agriculture. For the first time in history a policy of bumbling and fumbling has been replaced with a national policy for agriculture. We recognize the problem of the cost-price squeeze, the variability of crops from year to year due to weather conditions and fluctuations of price due to world markets and world conditions.
Our policy is a practical and workable one. Already the government has brought in the price stabilization act, increased farm credit, introduced cash advances, which C. D. Howe said would wreck the wheat board, amended 66968-9-16i
The Address-Mr. Slogan the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, initiated higher rates of compensation for cattle slaughtered due to contagious diseases and commenced the South Saskatchewan river dam after years of promises by the Liberals.
In this session we are looking with anticipation to the legislation on farm credit and crop insurance. But there are a few matters that are of grave concern to my constituents and there are some things which I should like to commend to the attention of the ministers. To the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) I wish to commend the extension to Manitoba and the western provinces of import controls which have been implemented in the maritimes against United States potatoes. To the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Harkness) I wish to commend the initiation of payment for farm storage of grain. It is only fair that in a time of surplus the farmer be paid for storing his grain rather than having the money go to warehouses and elevators at a cost of some one cent per bushel every thirty-five days.
I recommend that the farmers be allowed to load their own grain directly into box cars rather than having it go through an elevator at a cost of some four and a half cents per bushel to the farmer. These are not new ideas as they were first adopted by Dr. Manion and the Conservative party in the Regina manifesto of 1940. However, I shall present my arguments on these matters at a more appropriate time.
I have visited the various areas of Springfield. I have listened to the many problems of my constituents and my duty now is to do my utmost on their behalf. This I shall do, Mr. Speaker, through the proper channels as, unlike one of our former members, I do not want to be charged with talking my way right out of parliament in the same way, indeed, as the C.C.F. talked themselves out of the by-election in my constituency.
I feel very much at home in this chamber and this building because I have only to look at the walls about me to notice that distinctive and beautiful Tyndall stone that comes from Springfield. Indeed, in walking through the hall of honour and the hall of confederation I have noted that the main pillar which symbolizes the unity of confederation and the strength of Canada is constructed of that stone. I owe some thanks for my election to Tyndall stone. I did not allow the Liberals to forget that they had wasted a lot of money on the public printing bureau and, indeed, they had wasted a great deal of money on importing stone all the way from Virginia for that building, when they could have used the finest building stone on

The Address-Mr. Slogan the continent, Tyndall stone from Springfield. Yet the Liberals wonder why imports from the United States are going down. It must inspire a sense of guilt in the members of Her Majesty's loyal opposition each time they look at the walls of this chamber and each time the Liberals come into Springfield in the future and lament their attitudes, platitudes, and beatitudes, to the good people of Springfield I am sure they will blush a little for their betrayal of the people of Springfield and for having so little pride in the products of Canada. At this time, Mr. Speaker, I must also commend Tyndall stone to the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Green).
I come now to the opposition. I commend the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) for a fighting speech and, of course, no member from Springfield ever shirked a fight. I have watched the members of the opposition very carefully, and there is at least one member of that group who qualifies to be called a politician. As you know, Mr. Speaker, a politician is a person who approaches every situation with an open mouth. Indeed, this member seems to have contracted foot-and-mouth disease as well.
I should like at this time to make a few observations regarding the by-election in Springfield. I recall the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Benidickson) finding himself one night upside down in a ditch and, indeed, the Liberal party took an inverted position throughout the by-election. I am sure it brings no comfort to the Leader of the Opposition to know that one of their former Liberal members of parliament contested the Conservative nomination.

I am sure that the former
Liberal premier of Manitoba, who spent most of his time during the election repairing political fences in Springfield when he was not in the ditch himself, found no comfort when he saw that one of the former Liberal members of the legislature was also on our side in the campaign. I am sure that the Leader of the Opposition gets little comfort from reading such articles as the Canadian Press dispatch of February 27, 1958, which reported that Mr. Ben Nobleman, vicepresident of Trinity riding association, had resigned from the Liberal party and would support the Conservatives. I should like to quote the following from the dispatch:
He said he attended the Liberal convention in the hope that grass roots opinion would be heard but "came back greatly disappointed".
"Since returning from Ottawa I have been given the deep freeze apparently for daring to express my opinions. My role as first vice-president is rather farcical for I have not been consulted on any matters for the past month."

I am sure the Leader of the Opposition would like to know that several young Liberals have spoken to me and expressed their envy of the young Conservatives because they say that they do not have the same freedom of expression which we seem to have. I think it is this attitude on the part of young people all across Canada which has contributed to the large number of young members on this side of the house. I have been very active myself in the young Conservative organization and also as national president of the Progressive Conservative Student Federation. I have only mentioned this matter to ask the Leader of the Opposition to give the young people of his party a chance.
Earlier in the debate the Leader of the Opposition said that in some respects the Liberals and the C.C.F. may find themselves in some measure of agreement. Indeed, Mr. Speaker, the position of both parties is so weak that they may find themselves soon in a position of more than agreement. I should like to quote from an article that appeared in the Winnipeg Free Press of February 27, 1958. The article is headed, "Speakers Link C.C.F. With Tyranny." The dispatch comes from Regina and reads in part as follows:
Two speakers finked the C.C.F. with communism Tuesday as the throne speech debate continued in the Saskatchewan legislature.
Both these speakers were Liberal members of the legislature. The article goes on to say:
Mr. Barrie said no one admires what has gone on behind the iron curtain and under Hitler and Mussolini, "but we have had it in Saskatchewan and Canada for 25 years-they are celebrating the 25th anniversary of the C.C.F. this year".
Since its formation the C.C.F. had used the same methods of infiltration to gain control, including infiltration of non-political bodies.
Look at school boards, municipal councils, cooperatives and even church organizations.
Let me go back to the young people of Canada to see what is prevailing in the other political parties. I should like to quote an article appearing on the front page of the Winnipeg Free Press of December 13. I hesitate to bring this matter up because it concerns my own alma mater, and a matter that has recently been settled, in some measure, due to the good offices of our Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill). This article is headed 'Young C.C.F.er Charges Cynical Group Engineered Crowe Issue". It reads:

The Address-Mr. Slogan
A leader in the C.C.F. youth movement says a ''phony issue" has been created out of the case of Professor Harry Crowe because a small group wants to gain control of United college.
The Crowe affair, says Stuart Barber in a letter to C.C.F. provincial leader Lloyd Stinson, has been used as a "cloak" by this group to cover its "own brand of cynical bitter socialism".
The letter urges the C.C.F. party publicly dissociate itself from "the activities of some C.C.F. supporters" at the college.
Mr. Barber, a fourth year law student at the University of Manitoba, is a former leader of the university C.C.F. group and a graduate of United. He was this year's speaker of the university mock parliament.
I should like to quote a few lines from his letter because I think it demonstrates the sincerity of his belief in that party:
As you know, I believe that true democratic socialism can bring the greatest measure of happiness and justice to the people of Canada and the world. Indeed, I hope to devote some part of my life in working for the objectives of the C.C.F. movement.
What did the leader of the C.C.F. say after he received this letter? He disowned this sincere and critical young man by saying that Mr. Barbour did not have a membership card in the C.C.F. party. Well, sir, things are pretty tough for young people in these parties.
I should like to quote a few words from what Stanley Knowles said of the Liberals on December 17 just after the Springfield by-election. He said:
The Liberals are dead but they won't lie down. They can gasp a few more times before they finally die.
In the Winnipeg Tribune of December 8, 1958 the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) is reported as having said this:
The C.C.F. is a party which is not going to be in existence in a year and a half. By its own admission it is a dying, if not already dead, party.
At least, Mr. Speaker, these two parties think alike. Both of these tired old parties, which revel in the past and depression, conjured up the ghost of R. B. Bennett. They went about Springfield haunting the people, as indeed some members have been haunting the chamber today. However, they found the people of Springfield do not frighten easily. Indeed, the only ghosts about today are the ghosts of those members of the opposition whom the people of Canada have sent to a happier haunting ground. In fact, we have one lone member of the opposition from the three prairie provinces.
I merely bring these facts out to indicate to the opposition parties that we are aware of their plight and that we sympathize with them.

Coming back to the speech of the Leader of the Opposition, I should say I enjoyed listening to him talk for the speech was subtle in substance and fickle in fact. The hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) attacked our policy of positives with a nattering of negatives. Both these hon. members showed an obsession with recession and opposition without proposition. It is obvious from the speech from the throne that the motto of this government is progress not perdition, initiation not procrastination, legislation not agitation.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I hope that anything I have said will in no way be taken as a personal reflection upon any member, as it was not meant to be such.
I should like now to make some further observations. As I stand here, I cannot help but realize how great and diversified a country we represent. I realize that no matter how cosmopolitan we try to be, we feel a duty to defend our own provincial cause. But more than anything else in this chamber we learn to appreciate each other's point of view, for we can see the underlying unity in our diversity. As we meet today, we stand on the threshold of new frontiers, the frontier of the north, the frontier of the shrinking world and the frontier of outer space. Sir Winston Churchill said, in accepting the Nobel prize a few years ago, and I quote:
Today more than ever in history, events have dwarfed personalities.
Mr. Speaker, the destiny of nations lies in the personality of men. Today we are living through the pages of history. Today demand for leadership is as great as it ever was. Today, more than ever before, we need men of vision, of courage, conviction and perseverance like the father of the fathers of confederation, Sir John A. Macdonald. It was a Conservative government that bound this country together with the iron ties of he Canadian Pacific Railway against a defeatist opposition that ridiculed our policy as wigwam to wigwam. What Sir John A. Macdonald bound together no man has yet been able to pull asunder. The Conservative party has written the brightest pages of Canada's history in the past. The Conservative party will write the brightest pages of Canada's history in the future because it is to this task that our leader and our members are dedicated, as indeed all members of this house are dedicated.
The hour of 10 o'clock having arrived, Mr. Speaker, I should like to adjourn the debate.
On motion of Mr. Slogan, the debate was adjourned.
At 10 o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
